line: I was bored of education, left the town Fuck a résumé and fuck a cap and gown Fuck a background check back ’round when I get the check Nigga, that’s now

meaning:
JID discusses his disillusion with education, which he eventually gave up to pursue a rap career. He was a scholar, graduating from Stephenson High School in 2008. He attended Hampton University on a football scholarship, majoring in entrepreneurship with a minor in sports management. At the time, his future aspirations included college coaching, team ownership, and law school.

However, JID was expelled from Hampton at some point during his senior year and decided to fully pursue a music career. He rapped about his expulsion on his March 2017 track, “Somebody”:

I had got kicked out of school like, “Nigga, fuck y'all rules”
And them niggas that snitched on me, yeah, it’s fuck y'all too

After a concert on November 12, 2017, JID spoke with Hampton students about his experience and mindset following the expulsion, which Randall Williams wrote about in a March 2018 article about JID and The Never Story. JID told Williams:

[Rap] is my calling […] the money is great. don’t get me wrong. I love it, but I can rap my ass off, and the whole world gon’ know.

JID was literally forced to leave Hampton, Virginia and return to his hometown, Atlanta, Georgia, where he and EARTHGANG grew Spillage Village. These lines reiterate JID’s disdain for the commonalities of a typical career and state that the money he earns is most important.

line: Board of Education vs. Brown

meaning:
Brown v. Board of Education is a 1954 United States Supreme Court case that declared racial segregation of children in public schools unconstitutional. This landmark case was a focal point of the Civil Rights Movement, as it negated the “separate but equal” doctrine established by Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896. JID flips the typical pronunciation of the court case to rhyme “Brown” with the preceding line, “crown,” and the subsequent lines, “town” and “gown.”

Moreover, flipping the name can be interpreted as a critique of how educational institutions continue to mistreat students of color, more specifically African Americans, even after more than sixty years since the original case. This concept can be tied to the subsequent line, in which JID details his disdain for the damaged educational system and consequently leaves it.

meaning: Cole is reflecting on stepping out with his friends (“my niggas”) and feeling that “organic nostalgia,” a pure, unfiltered connection to the past — the times when they were younger, freer, and living on the edge. The focus on talking about conquests and hanging out in spots that “used to pop” captures both the carefree bravado of youth and the longing for simpler times, while subtly contrasting it with his present life of fame and responsibility. It’s a reminder that even as he achieves global success, there are pockets of memory and culture from his past that remain formative, grounding, and emotionally resonant — the energy of the streets and friendships that shaped him.

line: I’m livin’ my dream, my life is my childhood wish The guilt that comes along with that is the size of the rest Of the planet, I pray you get to see it across the Atlantic
vault_lines: I'm livin' my dream, my life is my childhood wish
The guilt that comes along with that is the size of the rest
Of the planet, I pray you get to see it across the Atlantic
Nostalgia that arouses when I'm with the rest of the bandits
meaning: Cole celebrates that he’s living his childhood dream — performing, traveling, and achieving what he once only wished for. Yet he immediately balances it with the weight of guilt, saying it’s “the size of the rest of the planet,” acknowledging that while he’s thriving, many people around the world (or even back home) are still struggling. The final line, “I pray you get to see it across the Atlantic,” adds both hope and distance: he wishes that those who couldn’t be part of his journey — family, friends, or his community — can witness his success, even from afar, showing that his victories are meaningful only when shared with the people he cares about. It’s a reflection of success intertwined with empathy, responsibility, and a desire to uplift others.

line: And while I feel powerless to change the power that is A part of me is yellin’ loud as shit, “You ain’t tryin’ your best” Too busy sellin’ out arenas and flyin’ on jets Life on cloud nine and I can’t deny it, I guess
vault_lines: Life is a trip, you can't predict the random way that it ends
And while I feel powerless to change the power that is
A part of me is yellin' loud as shit, "You ain't tryin' your best"
Too busy sellin' out arenas and flyin' on jets
Life on cloud nine and I can't deny it, I guess
meaning: These lines show Cole’s internal conflict between responsibility, ambition, and self-awareness. On one hand, he feels powerless to fix systemic problems or the hardships in his city (“I feel powerless to change the power that is”), acknowledging forces bigger than himself. On the other hand, a part of him criticizes himself — “You ain’t tryin’ your best!” — reflecting guilt or pressure to do more with his platform. Then he contrasts that internal struggle with the reality of success: selling out arenas, flying on jets, life on cloud nine, admitting he enjoys the rewards of fame even while knowing he can’t single-handedly solve the world’s problems. This tension captures the duality of gratitude and guilt, ambition and conscience, highlighting how personal achievement can feel at odds with awareness of collective suffering.

line: My mind is a mess, conflicted, ’cause their energy’s wicked Their need to impress at a high while their guidance is less

meaning: Cole is admitting that his own mind feels conflicted and chaotic (“my mind is a mess”) because he’s constantly absorbing the intense, harmful energy around him — “their energy’s wicked” points to aggression, envy, or survival-driven hostility in the streets. The next line, “They need to impress at a high while their guidance is less,” shows the tension between ambition and lack of mentorship: these young people feel pressured to prove themselves or achieve status, but they don’t have the proper guidance or role models to navigate it safely. It’s a sharp commentary on how environment and upbringing shape behavior, forcing people into risky patterns while leaving their potential unfulfilled.

meaning:
Depression and drug addiction are closely correlated, as someone who is depressed is more prone to drug abuse, and vice versa. It can be an extremely vicious downward spiral, as tolerances are built to the drugs being used, and the person is left to find a stronger and increasingly more dangerous medication to mask their suffering, as well as the complications accompanied with withdrawal. This can lead to an untimely death, as overdoses can occur when a person is far into addiction, intentionally or unintentionally. In fact, people who abuse drugs are 10 times more likely to commit suicide than the general population.

Unfortunately, it is often difficult to try to steer someone away from self-medication, as the attempts are often met with defensive behavior, as Cole recognizes in these lines.

Whether the person wants to admit it or not, these people are suppressing their emotions with drugs or alcohol, and Cole recognizes this. As a friend, it is difficult to watch someone you love go down the path of addiction, as it often leads to self-destruction. With the title of the song being “FRIENDS”, J. Cole capitalizes on the importance of helping loved ones find healthier ways to cope with their inner demons.

meaning:
Drugs in the inner city can be blamed on many different factors, including: economic condition, policies, policing strategies, hip-hop culture, violence, racism, lack of generational wealth (as expressed recently through music) and gun presence just to name a few.  It’s less cause and effect and more a tangled web of related actions and reactions.

Here, Jermaine begins rattling off some of these potential reasons for the drugs and addiction being present in his life and community, showing the complexity of the issue. The first and most obvious being the conditions he sees his friends in the hood are still trapped in. He notes the poverty, unemployment, and incarceration surrounding those he loves still back in Fayetteville, and in cities around the US.

One of main causes of lack of trust and increased violence in inner cities is the militarized policing strategies and lack of diversity in police departments. White cops from different neighborhoods end up riding around their jurisdictions armed and protected in their squad cars, in predominantly black and Latino communities, creating physical and physiological barriers between the supposed protectors of the neighborhood and the citizens paying for that protection.

meaning:
Cole brings up 2 prominent political names in this line. First, he mentions Donald Trump, mostly because his rhetoric has emboldened racists in the United States. Trump has been quoted many times for his oft-racist statements, which has caused many more people in America to agree with his discriminatory views. He has even infamously expressed interest in building a wall to keep Mexicans out of America, which stirred up controversy for the seemingly prejudiced views.



The Clintons' have been involved with controversy as well. Although the former president, Bill Clinton, had large African American support, he still turned around and implemented crime laws that destroyed people’s lives. His wife, Hillary Clinton, even used the term “super predator” to describe black youth, which shows that neither of these people give black people the equality they deserve.



Cole brings up these people as a subject for blame from many people in the hood. Whether actively trying to attack their community or using subtle racism to turn citizens against them, these figures are prime examples for people who suppress the needs of the minorities.

However, Cole may also be calling out those who blame their problems and lack of ambition on anything the first thing they can. The issue here is that they’re dodging their addiction and not addressing the obvious problem in front of them.

However, despite this rising epidemic, Cole knows he can’t comment much on the situation. Cole isn’t Jesus, so who is he to tell this people in what way they should cope with their problems and trials?

Still alluding to Kanye West, Cole questions how much effort was really put into The Life of Pablo.

Released on February 14th, 2016, the album’s tracklist and title were changed numerous times prior to its initial release. Much of the album was recorded within the final months of the album release, yet Kanye claimed he had started working on it as far back as 2014.

After the album’s release, Kanye continued changing it, calling it a “living breathing changing creative expression.” Kanye updated the album on TIDAL three times. He updated tracks with ones that had been mastered and remixed. He even added a new track, “Saint Pablo,” in June of 2016.

With a debate as to who should be crowned 1936 college football national champion, one columnist made a facetious case for Slippery Rock. His column was picked up around the country, leading to a buzz of interest in the small school. Boston University subsequently scheduled the Slippery Rock State Teachers' College for a 1937 match in Fenway Park, which was the first time Slippery Rock traveled outside of the Western Pennsylvania tri-state region for a game.

In 1959, the University of Michigan began including Slippery Rock football results in their public address announcements. It began as a gag but turned into a lasting tradition. In 1979, Michigan hosted a Slippery Rock vs. Shippensburg regular season game, drawing a crowd of over 60,000 – an NCAA Division II football attendance record.

Publishing rights refer to the actual music composition and are responsible for ensuring that songwriters and composers receive payment when their compositions are used commercially. Owning your publishing means you control all the rights to your music.

An example of how owning someone else’s publishing can be used as revenge can be seen with Michael Jackson and Eminem. That means Jackson continued to receive paid royalties on Eminem’s entire catalog until he died in 2009.

meaning:
Cole expresses his political disillusionment, arguing that politicians repeatedly promise “change” while the material conditions of poor Black communities remain largely unchanged, hence everyone still “floatin’ in the same old boat.”

He also questions how someone from his background is supposed to relate to the President when, in Cole’s view, those in power are removed from the poverty and neighborhoods they speak about. At the time of the song’s recording in 2008, George W. Bush was president. Bush came from the prominent Bush family, attended private schools including Phillips Academy Andover, and later attended Yale and Harvard, giving context to Cole’s claim that the President had never experienced being “broke” or living in the “ghetto.”

His refusal to vote and comparison of trusting the government to trusting “the Devil” capture the deep distrust of political institutions running through the verse.

He’s suggesting that instead of the deep, soulful connection they once had, the music has moved behind a digital paywall where it’s more about selling a provocative image and “content” than it is about the art itself. Under this lens, the genre represents a seductive and ego-feeding woman. She makes Cole feel like he’s the chosen one but that illusion is part of the game. And where love exists, jealousy inevitably follows.

That jealousy, rooted in the desire for her heart , or in other words the number one spot in rap, mirrors the 2024 real-life rap civil war between Drake and Kendrick Lamar, as both artists seemingly believed they were the rightful king.



Within this narrative Cole puts in an double entendre with having Drake’s “Best I Ever Had” – his breakout hit – mentioned.

JAY-Z also being widely known as one of the greatest rappers in the game, who was on top of the rap game in the late 90s to mid 2000s, which fits heavily with the ongoing theme.

Cole’s brilliance is in the self-awareness as he admits he was under the same spell (essentially fighting for the number one spot,) gassed/seduced by the same promise of supremacy which was promised to the other two by the metaphorical “woman”.

On the final and title track of the album, Cole rebuffs James' interpretation of a “real nigga” suggesting from his newfound perspective that James' commitment as a father instead is what made him a “real nigga” – and perhaps even immortal.

This could also be a potential reference to N.W.A’s “Real Niggaz Don’t Die” off of their final album together, EFIL4ZAGGIN.

Cole feels like living legends aren’t appreciated as much as legends who have already passed away. This could be the reason why he raps most of the album from the perspective of someone who is already gone.

Since all Cole wants is to be heard and make a difference in the world with his music, he feels like he has to decide between two options: die while he’s at his best and be heard, like Tupac, Biggie, and Eazy-E, or get old and have his best work forgotten.

Here, J. Cole references “range” and “a whip.” Obviously, he’s making a subtle nod to the hit video game Elden Ring, which features whips as a type of weapon that players can use.



Whips in Elden Ring are notable for their superior range when compared to other melee weapons — this is why Cole mentions “range” when talking about “a whip.”

However, whips have various shortcomings in Elden Ring, such as their inability to score critical hits or their general lack of variety compared to other weapon types, such as straight swords. In the context of the song, Jermaine says that the woman thinks somebody has the “range for a whip,” implying that she’s overestimating a potential partner’s good qualities. The word “range” can mean versatility, but by comparing this man’s “range” to that of a “whip,” J. Cole implies that his versatility as a partner may seem impressive at a first glance, but actually hides other shortcomings…he goes into detail in the next few bars.

Visionary rapping from J. Cole, seeing as this song was made in 2013, nearly a decade before Elden Ring released. This clairvoyance isn’t surprising, though. Cole himself has admitted to his awareness of the future early in his career.

line: Like a fuckin’ James Brown sample, you’re two-ever Times two, that’s forever, more treble Meanin’ more high-end shit on your level
vault_lines: Like a fuckin' James Brown sample, you're two-ever
Times two, that's forever, more treble
Meanin' more high-end shit on your level
meaning:
James Brown is one of the most influential artists in music history. This may be a reference to March 1970’s “Funky Drummer,” which is known as one of the most sampled beats in hip-hop.



J. Cole employs some clever wordplay here to suggest that his music is as timeless as The King of Soul’s ever-present catalog. He mentions treble frequencies, or the “high end” of the sound spectrum, in order to denote not only the crisp tones in his discography but the upper-echelons of success.

Prophecies that I made way back in the Ville
Fulfilled
Listen, even back when we was broke, my team ill
Martin Luther King would'a been on Dreamville

This year I’ll prolly go to the awards dappered down

Nintendo is a Japanese electronics company famous for its gaming systems. Cole speaks on the current generation of people compared to previous ones and how they would rather fiddle with lethal weapons—specifically  an “extendo,” which is slang for an extended firearm clip—than video games.

vault_lines: , I hope you can limbo
That chopper gon' spin you around like a judge on The Voice
meaning:
The Voice is an American singing show on NBC which first aired in 2011. Each season features four celebrity judges who go through preliminary rounds to find contestants to coach. In order to focus on the singer’s vocal, judges are seated facing away from the stage at the start of each performance; if they like what they hear, they can press a button that makes their chair spin around.




Alicia Keys pressing her button.

Cole compares this motion to the impact of a “chopper”—slang for an AK-47 assault rifle. His opponents will have to do the limbo in order to dodge his bullets.

line: 9. The Badness
meaning:
You say Im easily distracted I think the problem is Im easily attracted by the darkside
The temptation got me questioning where my heart lies
I’m tryna separate myself like apartheid
But ay the liquor keep swallowing
I swear I walk with God but the devil keep following

Cole is considered one of the greats for how much of himself he shows in his lyrics, keeping it real. In this song he talks about the highs and lows and how time changes: life itself as much as him. He knows he has two sides and try to separate them, as the Apartheid did (but this time around in a good way). He acknowledges his flaws and how much temptations makes it hard on him. He’s trying to do good, but his bad side is always a threat.

line: 1. Lights Please - Verse 2
vault_lines: 2. Dead Presidents II - Verse 1
meaning: I feel ya on this not being his absolute best. My choice was the second verse from Farewell, but it’s hard to deny the significance of this verse in Cole’s life and career.

line: 1. Lights Please - Verse 2
vault_lines: 2. Dead Presidents II - Verse 1
meaning: I feel this should be Too Deep For The Intro last verse

line: 3. Can I Live - Verse 2
vault_lines: 3. Can I Live - Verse 2
meaning:
Her sister on the other line talking to her shoes

This might be the best storytelling I’ve ever heard from J. Cole, and that’s saying something. I chose the quote above because I feel it embodies a lot of what makes this verse so great. It’s brief and Cole is describing a small action, but both of those things make it all the more powerful. The verse itself is describing a fairly large–though unfortunately common–action, but Cole’s descriptions of these small parts serve to make these characters and thus their pain real to the listener, rather than being able to divorce themselves and know that these people are just fictitious characters.

line: 5. I Get Up - Verse 2
vault_lines: 5. I Get Up - Verse 2
meaning:
We raising babies up in Hades where there ain’t no hope

This might be Cole’s angriest verse ever. He straight up calls out the president. I know other rappers have, but still, damn! This also makes it unusual for him, as it’s much more overtly political than he normally is. But it works out great. There’s so much anger in every one of his lines and you can empathize with everything he’s saying.

line: 7. Return of Simba
vault_lines: 7. Return of Simba
meaning:
This next shit is in no way to boast
But my city love breakfast, ’cause niggas had toast early
Coach had us doin’ jumpin’ jacks
Then sent us to the water fountain after runnin’ laps
My nigga went and grabbed his bookbag, threw it on his back
And brought it to me just to show me he was fuckin’ strapped
We was twelve years old, how was we to know better?
I analyzed his life and see that he was so set up

How can anyone say Cole is boring with verses like this?

Probably the least known of the Simba trilogy, it’s also probably the best. While the first two were good, the original had the aforementioned lack of a definitively Cole voice, and the second, while still better, didn’t display this level of tenacity or hunger.

Great storytelling, addressing some serious topics–both reflecting on his past and thinking about his future, and tons of wordplay (SO MUCH!), this track is a reminder of why Cole is considered by many (myself included) one of the leaders of the new-ish school.

line: 10. Farewell - Verse 2
vault_lines: 10. Farewell - Verse 2
meaning:
Got good grades but A’s can’t stop strays so pray for me

Off the top of my head, this is top 5 favorite closing verses on any rap project. This verse sums up everything great about Cole: great wordplay, like the quote above, tons of emotion, and a balance between the good and the bad.

Cole knows his childhood was rough and that he did some less than ideal things, but he knows that they’re what made him the man he is today. Because of that, he wouldn’t erase any of the pain or his mistakes; instead, he embraces and acknowledges them.

line: 8. 2Face - Verse 3
meaning:
“Don’t worry even Jesus never saw his real father”

Now that is how you do a fucking quote right there.

Cole spits one of his most famous verses in his mixtape, Friday Night Lights. He dropped gems, debating himself via happiness and pain from success, demons, money, greed and other factors.

From wishing he didn’t focus on stress when he should be happy, claiming he should have died instead of his homie, this is the Cole most fans identify with and why they stay with him for the longest. You can’t fake the emotions he put into this track.

line: 15. Lil Ghetto Nigga - Verse 2
vault_lines: 15. Lil Ghetto Nigga - Verse 2
meaning:
You kill a nigga over beef and cheddar even better
Just one less coon they won’t have to arrest soon

If you want a good picture of just how far Cole has come as an artist go back and listen to his first project, The Come Up. It’s rough, to say the least. He hadn’t really found his sound yet, production-wise, and at times the lyrics seem forced. This track was not one of those times, though.

While the production is dated, it’s clear that the subject matter is very close to Cole’s heart. Change up the beat and this could easily pass as a lead track on 2014 Forest Hills Drive. There’s a lot of raw emotion here, which is Cole’s bread and butter.

It’s hard to say for sure what sparked Cole’s emotion on this track, but it was released just a few months after a group of plainclothes police officers fired 50 shots into the car of Sean Bell, killing him and severely wounding two others, the night before his wedding.

line: 13. Heartache - Verse 2
meaning:
These niggas talkin' like they on the next level and shit
But Cole’s flow so cold, Bet the devil get sick

Warm Up Cole, showing his hunger and drive to be the best and get to the top. The lines above is just a great quote. Simple but effective. Rapping on a beat that’s not by him, he nevertheless makes it seamless within his mixtape and a track to get pumped to when listening.

line: 11. Let Nas Down - Verse 3
vault_lines: 11. Let Nas Down - Verse 3
meaning:
Reintroduce ‘em to honesty, show 'em that they need more
The difference between the pretenders and the Kendrick Lamars"

When you let an idol down, you are hit with pure depression. When that idol is Nas and been told he’s disappointed in you, that’s when you go out and try to make it up to him.

Cole puts his anger and problems out onto this song but the third verse is where he puts plenty of quotes. The above is my favorite mostly to how he treats his fanbase and as a rapper by keeping it real. He’s not in it for the money, he loves the craft.

line: 16. Rise and Shine - Verse 3
vault_lines: 16. Rise and Shine - Verse 3
meaning:
But if this shit ain’t fire, nigga, why you nodding with it?
The hate in your blood can’t stop your soul from vibing with it

A sarcastic Cole gets on his bragging game and, as this verse shows, his confidence in his abilities is well justified. Cole’s lyrical dexterity is on full display featuring impressive multisyllabic rhyming and plenty clever wordplay. Combined with a ferocious delivery, this verse really will have listeners' souls vibing with it.

line: 17. Enchanted - Verse 3
vault_lines: 17. Enchanted - Verse 3
meaning:
The devil buying souls, nigga, no refunds

Cole does what he does best here: vivid storytelling about inner-city struggles. Throughout the verse, he interweaves his own hopes and troubles with stories of some of the horrible things he’s grown up around. Near the end of the verse, Cole slows down to make sure every line hits home and makes fantastic use of repetition, first trying and failing to convince himself “ain’t nothing wrong,” and second, with the wonderfully simple “I gotta ball”—the urgency in his voice rising each time.

line: 19. Cost Me A Lot - Verse 2
vault_lines: 19. Cost Me A Lot - Verse 2
meaning:
Jacob the jeweler’s cooler now that he’s a felon

One of Cole’s most aggressive verses sees him at the top of his punchline game. Ruminating on the necessities of presentation in his business, Cole shouts out Waka Flocka Flame and addresses rap’s infatuation with villains.

line: 22. Breakdown - Verse 1
meaning:
When I say a minute I mean years, man
Damn, a whale could have swam in them tears fam

In the closing track off of Cole World: The Sideline Story, Cole discusses his absentee father and how it affected him as a child, a topic he rarely addresses. This verse shows why. Still struggling between anger at the absence and desire for affection, this experience has left a mark on Cole that he is not able to escape, even as an adult.

line: 25. Revenge of the Dreamers - Verse 2
vault_lines: 25. Revenge of the Dreamers - Verse 2
meaning:
No disrespect meant, honey, this just a compilation of my observations
While trapped inside this God-forsaken nation

This standout verse from the Dreamville label’s first official project, the Revenge of the Dreamers mixtape, sees the boss man lacing some stellar rhymes on a familiar topic: the hypocrisies of humanity. A common theme in Cole’s work, he takes a bit of a different approach here. Often Cole discusses his hypocrisies, but here he shows them in practice, angering a woman by essentially telling her he won’t sleep with her because she’d too dumb, but then trying to bed her later that night as he gets a little less inhibited.

line: 12. The Autograph - Verse 1
vault_lines: 12. The Autograph - Verse 1
meaning:
Ay, could it be I give the hopeless broke kids hope?
Caught me walking through the mall looking like he seen a ghost

This song couldn’t come at a better time. After the intensity of 2 Face, it’s nice to see this side of Cole. Often, it feels like he’s either trying to address major issues with appropriate seriousness or make damn sure people notice him. This verse feels like Cole couldn’t care less how people respond and is just musing on his life, how he got there, and what it and he might mean to others–I do love the anecdote about running into a fan. There’s no concern, just Cole taking a moment to consider everything.

line: 14. The Come Up
meaning:
And the clip is on E ‘cause your chest got a fill up

Probably my favorite song from Cole’s mixtape debut of the same name.

What makes this stand out so much is that Cole takes a break from the flurry of fast-paced rhyming that makes up the rest of the tape. While I love the rest of the songs and think the tape is mad slept on, a lot of it felt more like Cole imitating his idols than developing his own voice. This feels like it’s the first glimpse of the artist Cole later developed into: slowing down the flow and easing up on the need to rhyme as much as possible to make way what still probably one of his most quotable songs.

line: 20. 3 Wishes
meaning: I feel like this verse is a great example of how rap doesn’t have to be super technical to be amazing, something it seems like the fans and artists forget at times. Cole doesn’t rhyme a million syllables nor does he have tons of double entendres or puns or whatever, but the storytelling is so vivid and chilling that it gets to you, or at least me.

line: 23. Beautiful Bliss
meaning: I think it’s probably a combination of two things. First being that this verse is pretty old and even at the time wasn’t hugely well known, so I think a lot of people either forgot about it or never knew about it. Second is that, while it’s a great verse and was a big up for Cole at the time, I feel like he’s done what he was doing in this verse better since then.

line: 18. Tears for ODB - Verse 1
vault_lines: 18. Tears for ODB - Verse 1
meaning:
I’m here for more than just to kick some witty metaphors, dawg
This more of the type of shit you spit to set a war off

For me, this song marks the point of revelation in Cole’s story. He was tested and experienced arguably the lowest point of his career artistically after the release of Cole World, and while few considered Born Sinner to be much of an improvement, some of the material he released around that time showed glimpses of a much more mature Cole. This song is a shining example of that.

When I first heard this song, all I could think was that Cole had finally given up on trying to be the next Jay.

line: 20. 3 Wishes
meaning:
“Just trust me, don’t cry my nigga
The news call him a killer, but he my nigga
Sad shit
Ay yo genie last wish, free my nigga”

One of my favorite songs from J.Cole.

The melancholic beat allows Cole to flex his story telling skills. The three wishes refer to a genie granting him wishes. Cole expresses pain from his mother struggles, the inability to be a man, fighting back against those who done harm to his Mother. The heartbreak only grows when his homie gets convicted by killing someone. He tries to use his last wish to save him but he already used it up, leaving a dark fate for his friend.

line: 23. Beautiful Bliss
meaning: I’m surprised this came in at #23, tbh…This is one of J. Cole’s best verses IMO, and it’s a side of him that we don’t see very often at this point in his career.

line: 23. Beautiful Bliss
meaning:
Catch me on your doorstep you see me let me in
All I wanna do is eat I’m like the freaky lesbian

As 2009 came to a close, J. Cole was still reeling from a year that saw him go from just another dude with a mixtape, to a Roc Nation artist whom many considered the next to blow. What better way to cap it off than to renegade his closest peer at the time, Wale, on one of the most memorable tracks off of Wale’s debut, Attention Deficit?

This is arguably Cole at his hungriest, as he compares his punchlines to gut-checks and raps as if his success is all but guaranteed. Complex listed this verse at #23 of their top 25 verses of the past 5 years.

line: 21. Rich Niggas - Verse 2
vault_lines: 21. Rich Niggas - Verse 2
meaning:
But listen here I got a bigger fear
Of one day that I become you
And I become lost and I become heartless
And numb from all the Ménages
Just one bitch don’t feel the same no more
And Henny don’t really kill the pain no more

From Born Sinner, Cole explains his distaste to money and how those who have it use it to downplay anybody coming up or control them even. Selling dreams but the reality is not free. The extended quote screams how hurtful trying to become rich and famous in the rap game. Things you once believed were fun are now taxing. To the point J.Cole fears being fake, everything he claims he is not and finds the common anti depressants doing the opposite.

line: 24. Runaway - Verse 3
vault_lines: 24. Runaway - Verse 3
meaning:
“ If I follow my heart to save myself
Could I run away from 50 mill like Dave Chappelle?”

One of the standout tracks in J.Cole’s Sophomore effort, Born Sinner, he describes running away from the fame and music, to the point of suggesting that he managed to stay sane by making music and not hits. He wishes to be free but he’s locked away by the labels, so to speak, which makes the quote above that much more haunting. He’s running away from creating pop hits and trying to run away from the cruel world he’s a part of.

Who has the integrity to deny 50 mil anymore?

meaning:
Cole compares his paycheck to that of a celebrity lawyer: Johnnie Cochran, who helped former NFL star OJ Simpson when he was in the face of a murder trial.

Cole earns his wealth by telling people his entire life story, something that’s evident in Forest Hills Drive. Like most of us, Cole still doesn’t have himself figured out, and it frustrates him that a crowd full of strangers understand him better than himself.

line: And if you would like, I do it twice I just sharpen my blade, for a minute became lost in my ways
vault_lines: And if you would like, I do it twice
I just sharpen my blade, for a minute became lost in my ways
If you believe in God (If you believe in God)
meaning:

In the documentary Applying Pressure: The Off-Season, J. Cole emphasizes the importance of rigorous practice in honing his writing skills. He likens his approach to that of an athlete, particularly a basketball player, who engages in consistent drills to enhance performance.

Cole reflects on a period when he felt complacent, realizing that to achieve his full potential, he needed to dedicate himself to disciplined practice. This commitment involved setting specific goals and pushing beyond his comfort zone to elevate his craft. By adopting this mindset, he aimed to reach new heights in his music career, ensuring that he left no stone unturned creatively.

Humble beginnings!

Cole creates wordplay out of the word “pissed”, connecting it to literal pissing. Though his haters may be “pissed off” or angry, he suggests them keep it to themselves, which would be holding their bladder in the technical sense.

In football, a “lateral” is a backwards or completely sideways pass.



Therefore, a forward lateral would just be a regular toss forward. Basically, Cole is saying to keep your problems to yourself if you don’t want to get tossed in a fight.

Chapstick is a brand (and product in general) of small sticks of substance that keep the lips moisturized; hence not cracking. Cole figuratively extends this to express how he’ll never “crack” or show weakness.



This may also be a subtle nod to “Black don’t crack”, a comedic phrased used to emphasize how Black people don’t wrinkle and show age as much as other races.

Cole remembers a point of time when he was at a club near his hometown in Fayetteville, and gang-members he knew would have disputes with other people and they would open gunfire and shoot up the scene.

Toward the end of the verse, you here Cole’s voice shifting, alluding to Cole’s alter ego, “​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​kiLL edward” to show how he would’ve dealt with the pain.

meaning:
J. Cole’s upbringing was difficult, as he has detailed in many songs he’s written. Growing up in Fayetteville, NC, one of the most crime-saturated cities in the U.S., he endured many traumatic experiences that many people would find overwhelming and unbearable.

I grew up with nothin’. From them N.C. streets where killers hung at and slung crack for leisure

Because of this, he believes it would be difficult for any actor to portray him accurately, as many actors who play the roles of troubled characters become troubled themselves.

This also could be a reference to the previous line about “Shady” (Eminem), who played himself in his biographical movie, 8 mile. In this movie, Eminem played his own character because he didn’t think anyone else could portray his character in the movie as well as him.

line: Y’all niggas trappin’ so lack-sical-daisy
vault_lines: Y'all niggas trappin' so lack-sical-daisy
meaning:
“Lackadaisical” is a term that means lacking enthusiasm, apathetic, or lazy. Cole is speaking on the laziness of the current rap scene with the rise of mumble rappers and trap music in recent years whose subject matter is strictly drugs, women, and money. Notice how he enunciates the word lackadaisical incorrectly as if to make him sound lazy and uncaring like trap rappers do when they mispronounce words.

Cole would express almost identical thoughts on KOD’s final track, “1985 (Intro to the ‘Fall Off’)”:

Now you scramblin' and hopin' to get hot again
But you forgot you only popped ‘cause you was ridin’ trends
Now you old news and you goin' through regrets
‘Cause you never bought that house, but you got a Benz
And a bunch of jewels and a bunch of shoes
And a bunch of fake friends, I ain’t judgin’ you

Interestingly, the use of “lackadaisical” displays Cole’s lyrical uniqueness since no other rapper would even bother to match his vocabulary level.

Cole grew up in his hometown of Fayetteville, North Carolina.

In a study by Neighboorhoodscout.com, it was found that Fayetteville has one of the highest violent crime rates in the US, across any size of any community (large and small). The offences tracked include: rape, murder, non-negligent manslaughter, armed robbery, and aggravated assault.

Despite the heavy crime that plagues the city, Cole is one of few that truly loves his neighborhood.

One of the central themes of this album is drugs, considering the album cover, song content, and even the release date. Cole lists off many drugs that are commonly used these days. The ten specific words he uses in this outro all denote to the remaining ten songs on the album and their embodying themes.

Such illicit substances have the capability to control users through addiction and he places other things, namely power and money, amongst this same category of aspects in life.

Despite the drugs and these other two factors having such caliber of corruption, love itself can overcome any of these harmful realities.

This isn’t the first time J. Cole has mentioned “love” as being the strongest drug. On “Power Trip,” he rapped:

Ending off this track with love as a powerful theme fitly transitions into the next track, “Photograph,” that is namely on this topic.

Cole expresses irritation over the presence of newer rappers, possibly “mumble rappers” or those that appear to be imitations of him, as he claims that they are “cramping his style”. He also mentions “blow my high”, a phrase that means ruining the high one receives from smoking marijuana, essentially fitting in with the drug-filled themes found in K.O.D.

It’s also worth noting that Cole may be giving a slight nod to frequent collaborator, Kendrick Lamar as he may be referencing his 2011 song, “Blow My High (Members Only)” which mentions various narcotics such as lean and as the title implies, marijuana.

Nobody’s perfect, uh

Cole makes a cheeky assertion that he is perfect. He creates a play on words with the idea that if “perfection” was the offspring of “practice”, (if practice made perfect), then Cole would be “perfection.”

Actavis Generics is a pharmaceutical company that globally develops and produces over-the-counter medicine. Actavis was one of the biggest producers of Promethazine Codeine syrup, which is unlawfully used to make lean, or “purple drank”. Due to abuse, the product was taken off the market.

Actavis has made the bold and unprecedented decision to cease all production and sales of its Promethazine Codeine product. This attention has glamorized the unlawful and dangerous use of the product, which is contrary to its approved indication.

The effects of drinking lean consist of dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, and memory loss. Drinking this concoction results in feeling numb. In the album’s cover art, a child can be seen drinking the purple substance.

Bentley from his mama's whip
K.O.D., he hard as shit
meaning:
Jermaine—perhaps through a different persona—is boasting his excellent drug-dealing skills, something he’s done plenty of times before.

A “flip” or “flipping” is a slang used to describe buying cheap drugs and selling them for more. Cole subtly used the phrase once before in the closing title track of his previous album 4 Your Eyez Only:

Plus it’s hot now, the cops outside, it’s hard to flip a pack

“Keys” is a slang for a kilogram of any drug, typically cocaine. Being able to afford ten kilograms of cocaine by only selling a quarter of a “brick”—slang for a pound of cocaine—is pretty impressive for a drug dealer. Because of his astounding profit, he’s able to afford luxury vehicles like Bentleys.

This connects to how Cole stated in his secret showcasing of the album that K.O.D. stands for “Kids On Drugs” or “King Overdose”, along with the album being released April 20th or 4/20—a universally celebrated day dedicated to weed.

line: Platinum wrist ridin’ in back like Miss Daisy Platinum disc and I own masters, bitch, pay me
vault_lines: Platinum wrist ridin' in back like Miss Daisy
Platinum disc and I own masters, bitch, pay me
meaning:
Cole has released numerous albums, as well as songs, that have received platinum and/or gold awards. All four of his studio albums prior to K.O.D have gone platinum in due time.

In these lines, Cole also references the 1989 movie Driving Miss Daisy. The movie sees a black chauffeur from the South building a bond with one of his clients, an elderly Jewish woman. In a similar way, Cole has grown a love for his plaques.

Following the release of 2014 Forest Hills Drive, Cole ended his distribution deal with Columbia Records. Leading up to the release of the 4 Your Eyez Only documentary, Cole did an interview with NYT which revealed that he now owns the masters to all his music.

Gucc is a nickname for Mark Pitts, who was one of Cole’s managers. Pitts had previously managed The Notorious B.I.G., who is the one who popularized calling him Gucc.

Cole had already talked about Gucc’s quote to Vibe in 2011, just a few months after “Work Out” was released:

Mark Pitts said the greatest quote ever, I might get it as a tattoo one day. He said, ‘Play the game to change the game.’ It’s as simple as that, and it works for all levels that I’ve been on in this career thus far. Like, you come in with the intention to change the game, which I did and still have. But you can’t change the game until you actually get in it and learn how to maneuver through it. Build the right relationships, build the right fanbase, and get the right power. You get the power by playing the game. Those were ill words.

Gucc’s quote justifies how Cole took a more commercial approach for the lead single of his debut album. And while this choice disappointed Nas at the time, it arguably paid off in the long run. Cole’s early-career commercial success put him in a position to not worry about radio hits later in his career. His third album, 2014 Forest Hills Drive (2014), was released the following year with no pre-release singles and practically no promotion, and it remains his top-selling album.

I met Nas a couple times, but I just saw him in Toronto shopping and I ran to him. I feel lame as shit talking to him. When he bigs me up, it weirds me out even more. Like how can you give me props when you’re Nas? But when I talk to him, I feel like I’m talking too much like a fan. And it’s because I am a fan. So I’ll just be spitting shit out and then I have to be like ‘Yo just shut the fuck up.’ I’d probably be the same way with Jay if I didn’t interact with him so much.

To earn your stripes means to gain credibility in a particular field a.k.a. proving your worth.



Wordplay on stripes, as Adidas have stripes on the side of their shoes & logo, and are known as the brand with three stripes. Adidas has owned the trademark on three stripes since 1949.



Interestingly enough, on 2007’s “Quote Me”, Cole employs a different metaphor, likening his stripe amount to a zebra (Zebras have 22 stripes – a fact so widely known it inspired an experimental band), and comparing lesser people’s stripe amounts to Adidas:

We earn stripes, looking like zebras
Y'all looking like Adidas

meaning:
Cole puts his heart and soul into his music, making it his sole priority to deliver what his fans want to hear. Back in November of 2010 Cole dropped Friday Night Lights and his buzz reached a new high. However, his label refused to drop his album, and against the Cole’s wishes, so Cole continued to release album-quality music for free which he called “Any Given Sunday”, a series of EPs.



The first bar here is reminiscent of the opening lines of Jay-Z’s verse in “Never Let Me Down”. The titles of the two songs also closely resemble each other.

You don’t know what you’re missing if you’ve never had it. In the same way Cole hopes to open ignorant listeners minds to the more substantial branch of hip hop (like Kendrick) by drawing them in with a mainstream single and hoping that they listen further.



He also might be referencing the song by Kendrick called “Real”.

line: Yeah, and on this flight May I never lose sight, fuck it
vault_lines: Yeah, and on this flight
May I never lose sight, fuck it
meaning:
“Flight” may be a double entendre for his rise in success as well as his ascension in allusion to Christ’s.

Cole actually ran into Nas on a flight and played this very song for him. As XXL recaps a story Cole told to BET:


Cole described running into Nas in a Houston airport at six in the morning and showing him [“Let Nas Down”] just a few days after writing and recording it.

“I wrote the beat at the house, wrote the rhymes at the crib, and then I waited til I got to the studio that night to record it,” Cole recalls of the making of the track. “Three, four days go by, we got a show in Houston… I do the show, wake up the next morning, go to the airport at like 6 am.” While at the airport, Cole took out his laptop and handed it to a friend, still bugging out over the track, when his friend looked up and noticed Nas boarding the plane, eventually taking the seat behind Cole’s.

“Soon as I seen him I knew that this was fate,” Cole continued. “I was telling people, this album has so many moments that connected that let me know I was doing the right thing, and that was one of them… I give him my headphones—I’m trying to hear what part of the song he’s on, ‘cause he’s behind me. About a minute in to the song, he’s just like "whooo!” beating my chair, just bangin my chair. Overall he was wild, the look on his face was like, honored, honored that I would make that, and also highly impressed. So that was a huge moment for me."

Freedom or jail, clips inserted, a baby’s being born
Same time a man is murdered, the beginning and end
As far as rap go, it’s only natural I explain
My plateau, and also, what defines my name.

Both J. Cole and Nas say it at the same time, hearing more of Nas in the beginning and you hear more and more of J. Cole. Like J. Cole takes over the torch from Nas and he even talks in this song about the Nas comparisons.

By saying these lines with Nas, Cole also paints a picture of a fan singing along the words of an artist that they like…a lot. Cole says it with a laziness like he’s heard it a million times, but the inflection in his voice matches Nas, so it’s apparent that he practiced it like a fan would do their favorite rapper’s verse.

line: When he said he was a fan it was too hard to understand No time to soak up the moment though ‘cause I was in a jam
vault_lines: When he said he was a fan it was too hard to understand
No time to soak up the moment though ‘cause I was in a jam
meaning:
J. Cole met Nas while on tour and has always been a huge fan inspired by his music, but he couldn’t even fathom what was going on.

Maybe it was so outlandish he didn’t give it much thought since he was in the middle of so many things he was doing at the time.  On the other hand, perhaps Cole uses the word “jam” to describe a difficult situation, as he follows up in the next verse explaining that the label was sweating him to come up with a commercial single.



(J. Cole and Nas chilling at the 2013 Super Bowl)

Nas told Cole he was a fan of Cole’s music, causing Cole to feel disbelief at the notion that one of his idols he grew up listening to for years could now be a fan of him.  Cole states that being busy with tours and constructing his album kept him from realizing what made Nas become a fan of him in the first place.

The ending of the line “I was in a jam” is wordplay for a metaphorical ‘jam’ that someone is stuck in – a problem – and also alluding to the jam he was stuck in involved his label DefJam.

It’s unclear if the above paragraph is accurate, as it seems Cole has never been signed to Def Jam, nor have any of his albums been released under its imprint. But the album’s lyric booklet does capitalize Jam, suggesting there may be something to it.

A reference to the track “Big Brother” by Kanye West, which features the same line in the hook. It’s likely that Cole references this track for a few reasons:


Jay has become a big brother to him, in much the same way he was for Kanye early in his career.

I mean, you made "You Owe Me", dog, I thought that you could relate
meaning:
A reference to the Nas song “You Owe Me”, the lyrics of which consisted of Nas expecting sex from women since he bought them jewelry. The single is infamous in Nas' career as a failed attempt to ride trends by making a superficial club track rather than something meaningful.

Cole thought Nas would be able to relate to the industry pressures that led him to release “Work Out” since Nas lived through the same. This detail nicely shows the defensive, knee-jerk reaction that Cole has to the news.

Nas described his reaction to this specific line:

When I heard that [line], I was laughing my ass off—I was like touché. That’s my shit, for the record. But like I said in the remix, on my fourth album I got a lot of different fans that I’m tryna holla at. So you’re trying shit like that. But on album one is when you make that spark that lasts forever. It was a good album, though.

I went to Hell to resurrect it, how could you fail to respect it?
meaning:
In these lines we can truly sense the intensity of J. Cole’s agony for letting Nas down. Nas' is known for his saying “Hip-Hop is dead,” even using the saying as the name of his eighth studio album.



Cole has been through MANY struggles in his come up, and has symbolically been to hell and back, especially in the making of “Work Out.” Cole went to the dark side of rap (the simple, dumbed down radio side) in order to try and grab mainstream listeners, in hopes to bring them to the light of good music. For Nas to not respect that pains Cole to the point of dedicating a whole song to it.

line: Pac was like Jesus, Nas wrote the Bible
vault_lines: Pac was like Jesus, Nas wrote the Bible
meaning:
Although 2Pac is revered as a legend and the face of rap, Nas is actually the one who wrote the foundation of hip-hop. Nas' 1994 album, Illmatic is often referred to as the Bible of Rap, and many rappers credit Nas' flow-structures and lyrical storytelling as a blueprint for how to make classic hip-hop music.

Cole also used a very similar line in his song “I Got It” (2009):

And all hell, I started studying my idols
Pac was like Jesus, The Source was the Bible

“Pac was﻿ like Jesus” may also be referring the cover of Pac’s 1996 album The Don Killuminati: The 7 Day Theory, which shows Pac being crucified much like Jesus.



And Nas' “bible” itself could actually be referring to his Book Of Rhymes.

Also, he says this implying Pac was more well known and respected. While, Nas was underrated (hence no one knows who wrote the bible). He also shows how people live by the bible and look up to and follow Jesus.

J. Cole graduated from St. John’s University in Queens, New York in 2007, earning magna cum laude honors and accruing a 3.82 GPA over his tenure. He detailed his college lifestyle in his May 2007 track, “College Boy,” which was released right as he was graduating from school.

Cole spoke about his financial situation post-graduation in an interview with Interview Magazine in February of 2013:

Ah, man. Well, actually, I graduated magna cum laude. And after college, man, that was… Well, I was broke as hell. I was renting an apartment in Queens with my roommates during school, and after we graduated, they moved out and started their careers. I didn’t really have a career at that point[…] Well, I was hitting my mom up for money. I kept hitting other people up for money, too. I just felt like a bum. I owed thousands of dollars in rent and I was just waiting on my deal. My landlord was always letting me slide, but eventually I had to give him something, even just to show that I had income. So my homie hooked me up with this job at a newspaper.

Cole hasn’t forgotten that part of his life, however. He remains close with his aforementioned landlord, Mohammad, and even paid him back his missed rent and some once he got his deal.

line: Niggas wanted me to look the part, had to stop takin’ advice Put the jewelry to the side, had to find me, had to find God
vault_lines: Niggas wanted me to look the part, had to stop takin' advice
Put the jewelry to the side, had to find me, had to find God
meaning:
At the current stage of his career, Cole is known for his modesty and reserved persona. Some even say that Cole dresses like he’s homeless, something that Dreamville signee JID played off of in a skit on his November 2018 song, “Workin Out”:

Why that nigga J. Cole got all this money [but] look like he ‘bout to borrow somebody charger or something?

However, when Cole was still a rising artist, he often chose to dress like “the traditional rapper,” wearing expensive jewelry and clothing.



The most notable instance of this was Cole’s outfit at the 2013 BET Awards, pictured above. After two other artists wore the exact same thing, it became a public spectacle of “Who Wore It Best?”

Cole recalled this in his March 2019 GQ interview. He said that he wanted to wear something else, but the people around him were trying to convince him that the Versace sweater and chain were the things that would make him be perceived as a superstar, which is what he was longing for at the time.

Ultimately, this didn’t work out the way that Cole or those people had thought, which is part of why he came to the realization that he was doing things to impress others rather than being himself. From that point, he made a notable shift in his public persona that still persists. He doesn’t want to be defined by materialistic things or be perceived as vain. He also notes that he had to find God, which indicates that the glorification of wealth within the music industry may have initially deterred his relationship with Him.

Interestingly, less than two weeks before the award show, Cole had discussed his negative perception of materialism on his record, “Chaining Day.” It has also been discussed in several interviews and songs since the June 2013 event.

Cole talks about what he needs to complete before he can officially retire, or “fall.” He is telling his fans that instead of only giving listeners what they are expecting from him, he’s going to be completely transparent and tell as many stories as he can recall.

Since Cole unveiled the album’s title in April of 2018, fans theorized that The Fall Off was titled this way because it would be Cole’s final album and the start of his retirement. However, he had teased possibly retiring nearly two years prior on DJ Khaled’s July 2016 record, “Jermaine’s Interlude,” rapping:

Cole is now contradicting his previous stance as he realizes that there is more that he can divulge to his listeners.

Two days before releasing this song, Cole published an essay titled “The Audacity” in which he discussed several critical periods of his life. He also wrote on the times that he contemplated retirement before ultimately deciding against it. In the essay’s final paragraph, he wrote:

On my career bucket list, there remain a few more items to check off before I give myself permission to enter whatever the next chapter of my life may be.

It is still unknown whether or not The Fall Off will be Cole’s final album, but he seems to be preparing for the final stages of his career.

“Scar” could be connecting this line to the 1994 film, The Lion King, which inspired Cole’s alter ego and is where this song’s title is derived from. The movie’s main antagonist is a lion named Scar, so Cole could be saying that he wants to show his fans his darker side.

J. Cole calls back to his songs that have ridiculed the new wave of rappers, like his December 2016 track, “everybody dies,” and his April 2018 song, “1985.”

“1985” is the most notable; it was made in response to a trend of fans jokingly chanting, “Fuck J. Cole,” that was started by two Miami rappers, Lil Pump and Smokepurpp. The trend became quite popular and was even the title of a now-scrapped song by Pump. Cole eventually caught wind of what he perceived as disrespect, leading him to discuss his opinion on Pump and other artists like him. On one part of the song, Cole raps:

Following the song’s release, Cole and Lil Pump had an endearing conversation at Cole’s home in which they discussed the “Fuck J. Cole” situation and more. However, this didn’t stop Pump from falling off as Cole had predicted. Pump’s second album, released in February 2019, was critically panned and sold only 48,000 units in its first week. Pump will likely never regain the amount of attention or success that he had when he rose to stardom in 2017.

One of the other rappers that Cole was speaking to on “1985” is Pump’s friend, Smokepurpp. He has also evidently fallen off; his last release before this song, June 2020’s Florida Jit, sold slightly over 4,700 units in its first week.

Cole is also saying that he had the fatherly sit-down with Pump because he didn’t want to feel guilty if Pump had died a young death due to the topics of his raps.

line: Young Simba had the bustdown, yeah, the Lion King on ice
vault_lines: Young Simba had the bustdown, yeah, the Lion King on ice
meaning:
On this song, Cole is returning to his Young Simba alter ego, which was prevalent in the early stages of his career. It began with his May 2007 song, “Simba,” and he extended it with both “Grown Simba” in June 2009 and “Return of Simba” in May 2011. Prior to this song, he last referred to himself as Young Simba on his April 2013 track, “Head Bussa.”

For clarity, Simba is the main protagonist in Disney’s 1994 animated film, The Lion King; Young Simba is Cole’s way of juxtaposing himself with the fictional lion.

Disney on Ice is a series of ice skating shows that portray the company’s famous characters skating. There have been a few acts for The Lion King over the past few years, such as this one.

However, in terms of this song, “ice” means jewelry, as Cole says that “Young Simba had [a] bust down,” a type of diamond-encrusted watch popularly worn by rappers. Cole may be referring to the Rolex that Drake gifted him, which he briefly mentioned on his January 2019 single, “MIDDLE CHILD”:

Just put the Rollie right back on my wrist
This watch came from Drizzy, he gave me a gift



Cole wearing the Rolex that Drake gifted him

line: Gotta put ’Ville on the map, we forgotten
vault_lines: Gotta put 'Ville on the map, we forgotten
meaning:
Like several parts of this song, Cole is rapping from the perspective of his younger self. Here, he shouts out his hometown, Fayetteville, North Carolina, and reflects on a time when he felt that it was his duty to bring fame to the town.

Cole often abbreviates Fayetteville to (the) ‘Ville. He has referenced his hometown throughout his entire career, both in his music and other ventures. Cole’s record label, Dreamville, is a portmanteau of ‘Dream’ and the town’s name, and he has named songs after Fayetteville, including November 2010’s “Villematic” and December 2016’s “Ville Mentality.”

Cole uses the metaphor of a “mountain” that has simply “stopped” to describe his arrival at the absolute peak of hip-hop, realizing the cliché of it being “lonely at the top” is a literal, isolating reality. This sets the stage for his existential crisis: the struggle was his identity, and now that there is no more “up” left to go, he is left in a void where his massive success feels like a dead end rather than a victory, since he has surpassed his idols, leaving him with no ambition.

The lonely at the top phrase also leads into this because it implies that literally only one person can be at the top, so it is literally impossible to reach the top and share it with those you respect, making it a bittersweet peak.

This line serves as the emotional pivot of the song, transforming his long-awaited success into a “lonely” burden because the competitive fire he expected to find at the top has been replaced by the “complacence” of his idols. He’s finally able to “do the same shit” as the legends, but without them there to witness or challenge him, the accomplishment feels more like an ending than a beginning.

line: I’m tired of livin’ with demons ‘cause they always invitin’ more
vault_lines: I'm tired of livin' with demons 'cause they always invitin' more
meaning:
Negativity breeds negativity

Here Cole admits he has his own demons and they’re always trying to pollute his mental state and get him down.

This could also a Biblical reference. In Luke 11:24-26 (NIV):
“[24] When an impure spirit comes out of a person, it goes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.
[25] When it arrives, it finds the house swept clean and put in order.
[26] Then it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and live there. And the final condition of that person is worse than the first.”

Cole describes the task of dealing with personal demons, only to bring about new and greater ones. Fame allowed Cole to get out of poverty and support his mother, but now he has deal with the aftermath of it – the distance it has created between him, his family, and his friends.

The emerging concept that the “road to riches,” or path to a persons success that involves wealth, is a gift & a curse. You may have been able to overcome obstacles to reach your pinnacle, yet you most likely have not carried yourself in a good way to get there.

The prevailing idea is that people who reach a certain point had to do wrong by those they’ve come across because there’s no way to be successful and maintain integrity. He’s implying that on their road to riches they got what they wanted: riches. But they went about it the wrong way. This is the idea of “selling your soul” or to do something evil to obtain wealth.

He echoes the sentiment of getting lost in pursuit of becoming rich at the expense of happiness in his 2014 song “Revenge of the Dreamers”:

line: [Intro] You good, T-Minus?

This line went on to become T-Minus’s producer tag.

T-Minus earned the shoutout for co-producing this track with Cole, having previously worked together on “Kevin’s Heart” and 6LACK’s “Pretty Little Fears”, on which Cole is featured.

Here’s T-Minus’s Deconstructed video about the beat:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iBG2wv_Oook

Via Complex, T-Minus says this song was made “in one day” in North Carolina in December 2018 (about a month before the Revenge of the Dreamers III recording sessions in Atlanta). He also said:

[Cole] and his manager had an idea to pull a sample out, so we went online and we found this really cool loop.

The main sample is from First Choice’s 1973 song “Wake Up to Me”:

https://youtu.be/G8sbji10nu0?t=51

As noted in the Deconstructed video, there’s also a sound used that sounds similar to one used in “Window Pain”:

https://youtu.be/xmRde-gc0n8?t=63

The drums are super intense. T-Minus credits Cole for the 808, and he likens the drums to those on “KOD”, which Cole also made the beat for.

Cole is mapping out the universal struggle across every “side” of the city, using the Marvin Sapp interpolation to ground the chaos in faith. By acknowledging a “soft spot for the man up above,” he admits that despite the “hardness” the streets require, his core is still tethered to God.

He creates a stark contrast between those who “duck shots” (the survivors) and those who “catch slugs” (the victims), highlighting the thin line between life and death that exists regardless of your geography. For example, in 2014, Michael Brown was shot to death by a white police officer in Missouri as a result of a confrontation based on Brown being charged with a robbery. This event strengthened the Black Lives Matter movement, a movement designed to combat racial inequality and police corruption against Africans.

J. Cole has been known to be an avid supporter of Black Lives Matter and other racial protests; he dedicated a song, “Be Free”, towards Ferguson’s death in addition to touching this idea on songs such as “Neighbors”.

Some drugs, like cocaine, have been found to thicken blood by increasing the number of red cells and a certain protein that causes platelets to stick together.

Thick blood can also allude to loyalty and familial relationships, as the proverb “blood is thicker than water” means that family is more important than friendship. In an interview with The New York Times, Jermaine discussed his approach toward a more grounded lifestyle for the betterment of his family–he is currently married to Melissa Heholt and has a child. Another interpretation of this line is that it reflects the “alter-egos” that both superheroes and celebrities. The alter-ego of Superman is Clark Kent; Cole may be referencing how Superman slowly morphs into Clark Kent as he spends more time in society and integrates into his alter ego. Thus, Cole may be asking if the “heroes” or celebrities in life are nothing special and are all ordinary people but with more power and money which sets up for the themes of “Motiv8.”

Trayvon Martin, a 17-year-old black male, was killed in what was widely believed to be a racially motivated murder, which led to outrage across America. His murderer, George Zimmerman, was acquitted despite the clear evidence of his crime. In “Be Free,” Cole spoke on Michael Brown, another victim of a fatal shooting from a person in authority.

J. Cole lays out the mindset of Blacks in a country pitted against them, explaining the fear within Blacks to become a victim of America’s brutality

KELLEY: Who’s [B Nolan]? He’s the driver?

meaning:
The Japanese sample in question was likely the one used “January 28th”, which samples “Sky Restaurant” by Hi-Fi Set, a Japanese chorus group.

A sample in music is a portion of one song/composition taken and utilized in a different song (usually after some alteration).  Sampling played a major role in early and Golden Age hip-hop, from Public Enemy to Eric B. & Rakim.

However, sampling has been much less prevalent in hip-hop since the mid-1990’s.  In fact, after De La Soul was sued for an unauthorized sample on its “Transmitting Live from Mars” instrumental/skit, copyright law has required artists to get their samples “cleared” – or approved by the original artist/copyright holder.

In late November 2014, protests broke out in the town of Ferguson, Missouri when a grand jury made a decision not to indict white Ferguson police officer Darren Wilson in the shooting of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old black man who allegedly attacked the officer after being told not to walk in the middle of the road. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE ABOUT THE FERGUSON INCIDENT

In early December, Cole reportedly attended the protest in New York surrounding the death of Eric Garner, a black man who died after being put in an illegal chokehold by an NYPD officer who was not indicted for the incident.

meaning:
The outro is a massive “roll call” that serves as a physical map of Cole’s life. By listing specific Fayetteville neighborhoods like Tiffany Pines, Fox Fire, and Bonnie Dune, he is paying tribute to the specific blocks that raised him. The shift from “pay me” to “pay us” reflects a transition in Cole’s mindset; as he nears the end of his career with The Fall-Off, his focus is no longer on personal gain, but on the economic uplift of his entire community.

He expands this homecoming into a regional anthem by shouting out South Carolina cities like Charleston, Greenville, and Florence. By declaring “it’s the southeast,” Cole is unifying the Carolinas as a singular cultural powerhouse. He is effectively “signing off” by grounding his global legacy in the literal soil of the dirt roads and city streets where he first learned to hustle.

line: For some, that’s hard to believe Shout out the dog Petey Pablo, he did that long before me
vault_lines: For some, that's hard to believe
Shout out the dog Petey Pablo, he did that long before me
meaning: Cole pays homage to the North Carolina legend Petey Pablo, the rapper who first put the state on the national hip-hop radar in the early 2000s. By saying “he did that long before me,” Cole is showing humility and acknowledging that he didn’t build the NC rap scene from scratch. Petey’s hit “Raise Up” became the unofficial state anthem, and Cole views himself as the one carrying the torch that Petey originally lit. Calling him “the dog” ties back to the song title, “Old Dog,” signaling a passing of the guard between two generations of Carolina icons.

meaning: The “emblem” refers to the luxury car logo on his keychain—specifically the Lamborghini mentioned earlier in the verse. Cole is asserting that material wealth and status symbols don’t define his character or change his frequency. Whether he’s in a Honda Civic or a supercar, his identity remains rooted in Fayetteville. He views himself primarily as a representative for North Carolina, emphasizing that his success is a win for his entire home state rather than just a personal financial gain.

meaning:
Cole reflects on the historical struggle of North Carolina by stating “we never had shit,” highlighting a past defined by a lack of resources and recognition for his home state. He then declares that because “the GOAT” is now officially from there, those days of being overlooked are “past tense,” effectively rewriting the state’s legacy through his own success.

By closing with “We gas shit,” he uses a double entendre to mean both that they provide the fuel/energy for the culture and that they are “gassing” or dominating the competition, asserting that Carolina’s underdog status has been permanently replaced by dominance.

 By mentioning he is “accustomed to” this environment, he reinforces that his loyalty isn’t an afterthought of fame, but a core part of his identity rooted in the place he knows best.

line: It’s so precarious, so much random niggas clutchin’ tools It’s nothing new, they carry hammers into public schools
vault_lines: It's so precarious, so much random niggas clutchin' tools
It's nothing new, they carry hammers into public schools
meaning:
Cole uses the double entendre of hammers as a type of tool but also their shared connotations of being slang for guns.

Cole describes the environment as “precarious” because of the constant threat of violence, noting that many people are “clutching tools"—a slang term for carrying firearms.

He points out that this is “nothing new,” highlighting the grim reality that people are even bringing “hammers” (another term for guns) into “public schools.”

By using both terms, he emphasizes how normalized and widespread the presence of weapons has become in his community.

line: We on the map, we ain’t Atlanta, but we snuck on through
vault_lines: We on the map, we ain't Atlanta, but we snuck on through
meaning:
Cole highlights the regional expansion of his influence, noting that while they are now “on the map” and physically present in “Atlanta”, the central hub of modern hip-hop, their entry wasn’t through a traditional front door but rather a stealthy one as they “snuck on through.”

 This suggests that he and his crew established their foothold in the industry without conforming to the specific Atlanta sound or typical industry expectations, maintaining their North Carolina identity while infiltrating the game’s biggest stage.

It’s a nod to his “underdog” beginnings and the strategic, quiet way he built his Dreamville empire to eventually compete with the heavy hitters.

meaning:
Cole clarifies that being “real” isn’t defined by financial wealth like having “paper” or driving a “Benz,” nor is it about the status gained from “selling white” (cocaine) to clients who are “skiin'” (using).

He effectively strips away the common rap tropes of material success and drug dealing as markers of authenticity, challenging the idea that money or illegal hustle determines a person’s worth.

This is also related to the subtle insinuations of the tension between Cole and Jay-Z, considering Jay-Z is known for his Mercedes Benz references along with selling cocaine and Cole is saying just because someone has those things doesn’t make them real.

Cole World (World), Cole Life (Life), Cole Blooded

line: Right, right, right, right
vault_lines: Right, right, right, right

This repetition of “right” is similar to the one throughout Nas‘ 1992 track, “Halftime”:

(Right…) It’s halftime
(Right…) Ayo it’s halftime
(Right…) It’s halftime
(Right…) Yeah, it’s about halftime

It’s not a surprise to hear Cole interpolating a Nas track as he considers Nas one of his greatest idols along with stating his mixtape, Friday Night Lights, had a similar style to Nas'.

The very first track Cole released after KOD, “Album of the Year (Freestyle),” is over Nas' “Oochie Wally” instrumental.

Cole also dedicated a whole track to Nas on his sophomore album, Born Sinner, titled, “Let Nas Down”, which is actually a track where Cole vents his feelings about Nas' disapproval on Cole’s past single, “Work Out”, as he seemed to think Cole disregarded his lyricism and shot for a radio hit instead.  A few days after the release of the track, Nas responded back with his own track, “Made Nas Proud”, where he praises and relates to Cole.

Here Cole is suggesting that if some people (likely his detractors or rivals) were to take a lie detector test, the machine would likely indicate that they are being dishonest or deceitful. The “polygraph’ll probably pop” implies that the machine would detect and reveal their lies, much like a balloon popping when it’s overstretched.

line: My head envelops the pen, these ain’t fan letters I craft
vault_lines: My head envelops the pen, these ain't fan letters I craft
meaning:
Cole is likely using wordplay to convey a few different meanings. Here’s a breakdown:



●"My head envelops the pen" suggests that his thoughts and ideas are fully embracing and surrounding the pen, implying a deep connection and control over his writing.
●"These ain’t fan letters" means that what he’s writing isn’t mere fan mail or admiration, but rather something more substantial and meaningful.
● “I craft” implies a sense of careful creation, shaping, and refining his words, rather than just scribbling or writing casually.

Overall, J. Cole is asserting that his writing is a deliberate and thoughtful process, and what he creates is not just superficial praise, but rather a reflection of his own thoughts, experiences, and artistry. He’s signaling that his lyrics are authentic, personal, and carefully crafted.

meaning:
Throughout the second and third verse, Cole lays a personal diss aimed at a rapper from the 910 area code in North Carolina named Space, a local Fayetteville rapper and Cole’s high school acquaintance from Terry Sanford High School. Cole uses their shared history to dismantle Space’s fake character while contrasting it with his very own struggling upbringing. on “Safety” (track three off the same project,) from Cole’s homeboy perspective, this exact hometown beef:

Most of the city love you, though a couple seem jealous of your stardom
Like, what’s up with old buddy that’s makin' songs ‘bout you?"

Space fired first with multiple jabs throughout the years. In a move that circulated locally, he released a video in which he pissed outside Cole’s former Forest Drive 2014 home while freestyling a diss aimed at him.. His last public diss towards Cole came in the form of a track released in 2024 titled “Light Jermaine Cole,” taking shots at Cole for “selling out” and clowning him for being light-skinned. Cole flips it by recalling Space as a “geek” from high school who faked a gangster persona later, rolling with heat-packing crew, and adopting slangs & tattoos. Cole criticized this exact behavior from a more humble angle on “Window Pain (Outro)” from his 2018 album KOD where he rapped:

Niggas bang in the Ville, I always thought that shit was strange
How you claim blood or cuz when that was just a LA thing?
I don’t mean no disrespect towards your set, no, I’m just sayin'
That it seem like for acceptance niggas will do anything

He challenges Space’s street cred by exposing the fact that he was raised in a two-parent household. This may be a subtle interpolation of the iconic final rap battle scene in the 2002 musical drama film 8 Mile where B-Rabbit, played by Eminem, does a similar thing:

This guy’s a gangster? His real name’s Clarence
And Clarence lives at home with both parents
And Clarence' parents have a real good marriage

While going at Space’s neck, Cole references moving to Forest Hills Drive, domestic violence and starting to rap as his escape, contrasting it with Space’s fairytale bravado.

Cole then concludes with offering a fair fistfight back in the Ville, no hammers, to settle it mano-a-mano, with a nod to violence escalating signaling for curtains to close on violence (“when egos is flarin', beware that’s when they close the curtain”).

On another note, “getting shit off his sternum” means to getting something off his chest as in expressing his feelings and is a callback to his lyrics off “Stealth Mode,” an introspective track off his 2024 album Might Delete Later:

Nigga be steadily giving opinions
On shit that don’t even concern ‘em
