That's when I started rhymin' and makin' beats, son of a bitch
meaning:
Cole reflects on a pivotal shift in his childhood. Before moving to Forest Hills Drive in Fayetteville, he and his family lived in cramped houses and trailer parks in rough neighborhoods, environments he’s described as “super hood.” The move initially brought peace, stability, and a sense of upward mobility, made possible when his mother remarried and the household gained a second income.

That peace was short-lived. Cole has spoken about domestic abuse in the home involving his stepfather, which affected his mother, his brother, and himself. When he says “a key just switched,” he’s describing the psychological turning point where that trauma ignited a deeper urgency within him, the realization that he had to become “something” to escape his circumstances.

That moment marked the beginning of his artistic path. Music became both an outlet and a lifeline, pushing him to start rapping and making beats as a way to process his environment and envision a better future.

Cole sitting atop his childhood home on Forest Hills Drive, the house that inspired his 2014 magnum opus 2014 Forest Hills Drive.

WarGames is a 1983 American techno-thriller film that follows the story of David Lightman, a high school hacker. Lightman tries to access video games and ends up inadvertently discovering a back door into a military central computer.

In WarGames, when it comes to war, the only way to win is not to play. Cole may be alluding to the film’s classic theme, where his younger self’s attempts to “play the game” do not lead to success but instead bring pain to himself and others.

In his January 2019 hit “MIDDLE CHILD,” Cole famously rapped:

If I smoke a rapper, it’s gon' be legit

Leaning back into this sentiment, Cole explains his infamous decision to forfeit the high profile beef between Kendrick Lamar and Drake. After Lamar dissed both Cole and Drake on March 2024’s “Like That” by Metro Boomin, Cole replied weeks later with his April 2024 diss track “7 Minute Drill.” In it, he mocked Lamar’s discography quality and career trajectory.

Not even 48 hours after the song’s release to a notably negative reception, Cole would publicly apologize for the track and insist on removing it from streaming platforms during his performance at Dreamville Fest 2024 on April 7th. He essentially confessed that the track came from a place of insincerity and peer pressure:

I was conflicted because, one, I know my heart and I know how I feel about my peers – these two niggas that I just been blessed to even stand beside in this game, let alone chase they greatness. So, I felt conflicted ’cause I’m like, ‘Bruh I don’t even feel no way.’ But the world wanna see blood. I don’t know if y’all can feel that, but the world wanna see blood. […] I moved in a way that I spiritually feel bad on. I tried to jab my nigga back and keep it friendly, but at the end of the day, when I listen to it and when I see the talk, that shit don’t sit right with me with my spirit. That shit disrupts my fucking peace. So what I want to say right here tonight, is that in the midst of me doing that – trying to find a little angle and downplay this nigga’s catalog and greatness – how many people here think Kendrick Lamar is one of the greatest motherfuckers to ever touch the fucking microphone? […] I ain’t gonna lie to y'all, [the] past two days felt terrible, like, it let me know how good I been sleeping these past ten years. […] We taking that song off of fucking streaming services, nigga.

While many indicted this as an act of cowardice, Cole insists that he did it to avoid the figurative “bloodshed” he foresaw it amounting to. From allegations of pedophilia and parental negligence to mocking traumas and allegations of spousal abuse, the feud saw both Lamar and Drake go to extremely disrespectful measures that Cole didn’t want to feel obligated to partake in.

He also finds it rather strange that people would accuse him of “dodging smoke” or fearing lyrical competition when he showed off the “fire in [his] pen” or lyrical talent before, during, and after the beef. Prior to the beef, he was in the midst of a celebrated run of features lasting from late 2023 to early 2024. Might Delete Later, Cole’s 2024 project that “7 Minute Drill” was removed from, showcases some of his most lyrically dense verses to date. He’d continue his streak of features during and after the beef with April 2024’s “Red Leather” and September 2024’s “Ruby Rosary.” To ignore this context to push a narrative is dishonest in his eyes.

Perhaps in reflecting upon this fallout, Cole is content in knowing that he chose to preserve two cherished friendships in Lamar and Drake over giving into the pressure of the public and “going for blood” for the validation of bad faith instigators.

line: Niggas know a verse from Cole be like a signed Michael Jordan rookie card in mint condition

meaning:
Cole equates his verses to one of the most valuable collectibles in sports memorabilia, a signed Michael Jordan rookie card.

A rookie card is the first official trading card released for an athlete at the start of their professional career. These are typically the most valuable because they mark the beginning of a legendary career.

Michael Jordan is widely regarded as one of the greatest basketball players ever, and his rookie cards (especially from 1986 Fleer) are among the most iconic in trading card history. A signed version in mint condition (flawlessly preserved) is very rare. In 2025, a ’86 Fleer Jordan autographed rookie card was reportedly sold for around $2.7 million. I’m sorry Cole but I would rather have the card.

line: Your shit ain’t addin’ up, know you a phoney, checked your image Rappin’ tough, but all them niggas in your audience is bitches And white boys mostly,

Rappin' tough, but all them niggas in your audience is bitches
And white boys mostly,
meaning:
A subliminal shot at Kendrick Lamar following the fallout from “Like That,” where Kendrick dissed both Cole and Drake, igniting the 2024 rap civil war.

Cole critiques Kendrick Lamar’s fanbase demographics, suggesting it skews heavily toward women and white listeners. This can be seen as a disconnect between Kendrick’s image as a socially conscious rapper championing Black struggle and culture, and the reality that his content is mainly consumed by audiences outside the culture it represents.



This critique is reinforced by Kendrick’s crossover collabs with mainstream white pop acts like Taylor Swift and Maroon 5, which detractors use to argue that his appeal extends heavily into white pop audiences, potentially damaging the “for the culture” image.



Notably, this isn’t just Cole’s angle, Drake would use a similar line of attack on “Family Matters” and “Push Ups,” questioning Kendrick’s authenticity.

line: [Verse]

meaning:
While listening to this verse, it is hard not to compare it to Kendrick Lamar’s “How Much A Dollar Cost” off of To Pimp A Butterfly. There are many striking similarities between the two tracks, and it is easy to believe that Cole drew inspiration from it:


Cole and Kendrick are both pictured filling up their car at a gas station.
Both refer to themselves as big in someway. In Cole’s case, it’s because he is much taller than the average man (6 feet 3 inches), and Kendrick feels big coming out of his luxury car, “Hopping out feeling big as Mutombo”.
Both are somewhere foreign to them, as Cole raps “I pulled into this lil' station that I had seen on the ave'
In a peculiar hood, in unfamiliar paths”. And as we know from To Pimp A Butterfly, Kendrick was mainly inspired by his 2014 trip to South Africa, to where many themes and events originated from.
Both are approached by a man who is smoking (marijuana for Cole, crack for Kendrick) and asks them for something. Here, the man wants to take his time to appreciate the impact Cole’s music had on him, and asks him for a picture to show how much Cole means to him. On How Much A Dollar Cost, the man approaching Kendrick asks for a dollar, with the song later revealing that the man is God, and came to Kendrick to see whether or not he deserved a spot in heaven.
Not related to How Much A Dollar Cost, but still relevant: on several bars, Cole employs the same flow, cadence and word punctuation used by Kendrick Lamar and YG on their 2014 collab song  “Really Be (Drinkin' N Smokin')

Cole presents a stark look at the cycle of stagnation that often traps successful artists. By grouping “making beats” and “gettin' high” with “chasing freaks,” he’s effectively devaluing the typical rap superstar lifestyle. He is pointing out the irony of “feeling fine” while being stuck in a loop; it’s a comfortable numbness where the thrill of the hustle has turned into a predictable, daily routine.

The phrase “change our ways” suggests that Cole is feeling a moral or creative weight. He’s acknowledging that doing the “same thing we did yesterday” is the enemy of growth. It’s a moment of mid-career clarity where he realizes that if he doesn’t evolve past these surface-level habits, he’s just running in place, regardless of how much money is in the bank.

This chorus is a direct interpolation of Devin the Dude’s “Just Tryin ta Live.”

A theme throughout the album is the disillusionment that comes with ultimate success. On the aptly titled “Lonely at the Top,” Cole laments how being one of the most praised, commercially successful rappers ever leaves him feeling unfulfilled despite the exhausting effort he’s put into achieving that status.

This creates a dramatic irony in how this seemingly small, “quick” interaction with a fan reminds Cole of the true significance of his life’s work: The difference his music makes for everyday people. Whether it be the grieving little girl he aided through his charity foundation whom he spotlighted on his 2018 finale “Window Pain (Outro)” or the homeless man who wrote a letter to Cole about how his 2014 hit “Love Yourz” stopped him from committing suicide, Cole’s music is celebrated for how it uplifts the most downtrodden of people.

Cole recognized exactly this on his 2024 track “Port Antonio” after reflecting on “losing” the viral 2024 rap “civil war” and the toll it took on the “picture painted” of him, i.e. his reputational image:

Tappin' back into your magic pen is what’s imperative
Remindin' these folks why we do it, it’s not for beefin'

Help you cope with the rough times and shit

“‘Til you forget who you is, and you forget who you ain’t” might be an interpolation of 2000 hit “So Fresh, So Clean” by OutKast where André 3000 famously raps:

Cole samples this exact line in the outro of “Farewell” from his 2010 mixtape Friday Night Lights.

vault_lines: Hit and run, bigger funds

line: Yeah, who can hold us? Super focused
vault_lines: Yeah, who can hold us? Super focused

line: Money comin’ soon, tell my niggas, “Be patient”
vault_lines: Money comin' soon, tell my niggas, "Be patient"

line: I’m talkin’ reckless What you expect, nigga? I’m flexin’
vault_lines: What you expect, nigga? I'm flexin'
meaning: He’s breaking the fourth wall. He acknowledges that his tone is aggressive and arrogant, but justifies it as a natural byproduct of his “flexing” (showing off his talent).

line: What up then? Niggas ain’t sayin’ nothin’? Shut up then
vault_lines: What up then? Niggas ain't sayin' nothin'? Shut up then
meaning: This mimics a real-life confrontation. Cole is mocking the silence of his haters, using the pause in the beat to highlight their lack of a response.

line: ’Bout that paper, we could give a fuck if you believe us
vault_lines: 'Bout that paper, we could give a fuck if you believe us
meaning: Cole is dismissing the need for external validation. As long as the money is coming in and his family is fed, the “opinions” of industry insiders don’t matter.

line: Got beef? Come meet us, okay, I thought so
vault_lines: Got beef? Come meet us, okay, I thought so
meaning: Another “rhetorical” challenge. He’s calling the bluff of anyone claiming to have a problem with him, emphasizing his confidence in his squad. Beef is also a type of meat (‘meet’).

line: Y’all niggas are so mad ’cause I floss so bad on bitches
vault_lines: Y'all niggas are so mad 'cause I floss so bad on bitches

line: So I do what’s best for me
vault_lines: So I do what's best for me

But we also callin' that shit Dreamville
meaning: Fayetteville, North Carolina, is J. Cole’s hometown. Fayettenam is a portmanteau of Fayetteville and Vietnam. According to a report by The Fayetteville Observer, the name colloquially caught on around the ‘60s and '70s while the Vietnam War  was in full swing because of Fayetteville’s high volume of criminal activity. The nickname has lessened in popularity, but people like Cole still use it to signal the harsh realities of his city, even if it’s not as it was in the '60s/'70s.

Cole connects this to how big industries make deals with aspiring artists. meaning:
The phrase “One time for my granny up in heaven tonight” is a way of paying tribute or showing respect to someone’s grandmother who has passed away and is believed to be in heaven. Here’s a breakdown of the statement:

“One time for”: This phrase is often used in a celebratory or honoring context, suggesting that the speaker is dedicating a moment or an action to someone or something. In this case, it’s for the speaker’s grandmother.

“my granny up in heaven tonight”: This part acknowledges that the speaker’s grandmother is no longer alive and has passed away, but they believe that she is in heaven. It’s a common sentiment to express that a loved one who has passed away is now in a better place, which, in many cultural and religious beliefs, is often symbolized as “heaven.”

So, when someone says, “One time for my granny up in heaven tonight,” they are taking a moment to remember and honor their deceased grandmother, expressing love, respect, and possibly even a wish that she is happy and at peace in the afterlife. It’s a way of keeping the memory of their loved one alive and showing that they are still thinking about and cherishing their grandmother’s presence, even though she is no longer physically with them.

“12,” “Jake,” and “Five-O” are all common slang terms for the police. The repeated use of “still” highlights that Rocky’s negative feelings toward law enforcement have remained consistent over time. Following a physical altercation in Stockholm, he was detained in a Swedish prison for nearly a month and later found guilty of assault. The case drew widespread media attention, with many feeling that Rocky was treated unfairly by the legal system. This personal encounter with the justice system likely deepened his skepticism of law enforcement, reinforcing the defiant sentiments expressed in this line. line: Fayettenam,
meaning:
“Fayettenam” is a derogatory nickname for Fayetteville, North Carolina, Cole’s hometown, that emerged during the Vietnam War era. The name draws a comparison to the war, as Fayetteville (located next to the military base of Fort Bragg) struggled with high crime rates during the 1960s and 70s.

This is the last (so far) of several mentions of “Fayettenam” in Cole’s discography. Other songs where the nickname is mentioned include “Villematic”, “Farewell”, “Dead Presidents II”, “Last Call”, “I’m the Man”, “Throw It Up” and “Visionz of Home”.

line: Runaway, runaway Runaway, runaway I’m holdin’ on Desperately Runaway, runaway Runaway, runaway I’m holdin’ on
meaning:
The hook, at this point, trails the question that Cole posed at the end of Verse 3, wondering if he’d be able to run away from a lucrative deal at the cost of losing his artistic integrity.

In a sense, the word “runaway” that is repeated in the hook at this point refers to actually doing the honorable thing, maintaining J. Cole’s true sense of self and not being bought, whereas during the rest of the song, “running away” was associated with less principled behavior, like indulging in his unrestrained desires at the cost of cheating on his faithful woman.

This could be interpreted as him, by the end of the song, finally learning to own up to doing the noble thing
or…
it could be interpreted as him still being selfish and not compromising his self-serving behavior, even for the possibility of making 50 million dollars. It could be argued that maintaining one’s own artistic integrity is not necessarily a selfless thing. It is perhaps axiomatically selfish behavior… though that’s an argument for another time.

In all fairness, it’s likely that “running away” at this point simply refers to running away from situations that a person isn’t comfortable dealing with, like Chappelle having to continue a show that wasn’t sending the message he wanted to send or like a black slave having to take care of a child that was made through slaveowner rape. Would he have the power to run away from these situations, knowing that it’s probably practical to stay?

line: As we slave for peasant wage with no nest egg saved for rainy days
vault_lines: As we slave for peasant wage with no nest egg saved for rainy days
meaning:
This line is a double entendre
A play on the words peasant/pheasant as a near-homophone.

“for peasant / pheasant wage”

This is the hinge of the line.
• Peasant wage: barely enough to survive; historical poverty; class immobility.
    • Pheasant wage (by sound): pheasant isn’t paid — it is hunted, served, consumed.

So the phrase can be heard two ways at once:
1.  We are paid like peasants — poorly.
    2.  We are compensated like pheasants — not compensated at all, merely used.

The wage itself becomes suspect. Is it payment, or just the minimum necessary to keep the “game” alive for the next hunt?

“with no nest egg”

This seals the metaphor.

A nest egg is literally an egg kept safe so life can continue.
But pheasants lay eggs in nests — and those eggs are often:
• taken
• destroyed
    • never allowed to mature

So “no nest egg” now means:
• no savings for the future (economic reading)
    • no protected space for growth or reproduction (biological / animal reading)

In other words: the system not only exploits labor, it prevents continuity — no generational safety, no future leverage, no escape.

Putting it all together:

We labor like slaves, are compensated as peasants, treated like pheasants, and denied even the basic conditions needed to secure a future.

Cole’s one-night stand is tempting him. “Pie” is an euphemism for the women’s private parts. Comparing female genitalia with apple pie in particular has been notoriously introduced to popular culture in the movie American Pie.

But the apple also connects to the sin Adam and Eve commit in the Bible, Book of Genesis, when they eat from the “forbidden fruit”. Similarly, tasting from the woman’s forbidden fruit, her apple pie, would be a sin – not only because Cole has a girl at home.

This further connects to the album’s theme of Cole being a born sinner and also foreshadows the upcoming track “Forbidden Fruit”, which is about enjoying sexual pleasure and likewise mentions apple juice falling from a woman’s (lower) lips.



The apple pie could also represent the American Dream of being successful. J. Cole is trying so hard to pursue this dream, but he’s having a hard time resisting the temptation associated with being famous.

It’s also a simple reference to how being high often comes with having the munchies.

The nickname has lessened in popularity, but people like Cole still use it to signal the harsh realities of his city, even if it’s not as it was in the '60s/'70s.

He wants to make sure that his detractors understand that they are hating on the future of rap. He knows that he has a bright future ahead of him and refuses to allow his haters to get the best of him.

He later echoes a similar sentiment on the track, “I’m the Man,” when he raps:

I hear you all little niggas talking, nigga
Prince of the city, nigga
Prince of the south, nigga, holla at me

He believes that he is the future successor to the king of rap and that it is useless to argue with others, when he is likely going to be richer than them anyways.

Cole also implies that he is famous in the streets, and that his beats/rhymes are the reason for his success. He believes that his material is consistent to his real life experiences and that he raps for the people on the streets.

Another interpretation of the line is that Cole is actually in the underworld. Hell is typically depicted as a red place, similar to Mars. Mars has a orange-reddish appearance due to the high concentration of iron oxide particles in there.

This may also allude to his basketball career. Cole actually walked-on to the St. John’s University. He believed that he could have went on to play professionally but was set back due to some obstacles he faced when he was younger. In an interview with Bleacher Report, he said:

I was always in love with basketball as a kid, but I thought I was way better than I really was, because I didn’t have a male figure around to show me how to actually play. Me and my brother just kind of figured it out playing rec ball. I went to a middle school that didn’t have a team. That kind of set me back.

meaning:
Continuing in his discussion of Chicago multi-genre artist Noname, Cole explains that she may have had a “head start” in her social awareness from an upbringing that incorporated education on Black liberation in America into the way she was raised.

However, Noname has discussed her familial upbringing in multiple interviews during her career, and revealed that she grew up with her grandparents on the South Side of Chicago until she was 13 and after moved in with her mother. She delved deeply into her upbringing in a February 2017 interview with the Chicago Tribune:

[My grandmother was] the woman who raised me until I was about 13, 14. My mother owned a bookstore, which she started when she was 24 (in 1991), the same age when she had me, and she ultimately didn’t have time to juggle both the store and raising me — she didn’t know how. She was young and a new entrepreneur, and for her it made sense for me to stay with my grandmother. I saw my mom on weekends. My grandparents had full custody, and my mom was like a visiting relative. Once things slowed down with my mother’s business, I moved back in with her. It was a little strange at first, there was a little resentment, because I took to my grandmother a little more. So when I moved in with my mother, it was a little awkward, but we’re good now.

One interesting part of her youth that Noname frequently addresses is her participation in the Chicago youth media group YOUmedia, where she met and befriended fellow Chicago rappers such as Chance the Rapper, Saba, Cam O'bi, and others. On her participation in the group, Noname said:

[YOUmedia] was my safe place to create and feel understood in a lot of ways, to feel like I could create openly, with vulnerability and not to be judged or criticized… [The transition from poetry to rap] wasn’t hard — the environment was so filled with a variety of art forms. There would be someone singing, rapping, reading a poem, doing a short monologue or dancing — it was like a variety show. Being around a bunch of different people who were rapping, I felt like I could do both. We’d have these cyphers after each open mic.

The stories and perspectives that each of her fellow participants may have rubbed off on her during the youth program may have helped give her confidence in both her musical and social voice, allowing her to be as much of an advocate for change that she is now.

meaning:
While the exact timeline of slavery in the Americas is unknown, African slaves are estimated to have been first brought to America by Spanish and Portuguese settlers somewhere from 1501 – 1505. Slavery in America was officially abolished on December 18, 1865 by the Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, giving the total duration of slavery in the United States a range of 360 to 364 years.

Cole compares the physical shackles African slaves experience while coming to America to the restrictions that systemic racism in America have on the mindset of Black people in the country. Having been oppressed for the many years and having heard many stories of oppression from past generations, Cole says Black people in America are unable to believe that there is an escape from the subjugation that they experience in society, stressing the importance to free themselves from this restriction before further change can be made.

Cole then gives his own input on how education on racial discrimination and inequality should be undertaken in America, saying that it should be a gradual process and cannot be an undertaking completed overnight. He also says education on the topics in communities should start within the communities themselves, allowing people to gradually rid it from their own community and eventually removing it from the country altogether.

This is a stark contrast from Noname’s strategy on education, as she speaks loudly on the issues on her various social media accounts.

meaning:
Snow on tha Bluff is a January 2011 movie about Curtis Snow, an Atlanta robber and crack dealer who, in the film, stole a camera from college kids during a drug deal and made an autobiographical documentary.

The film was so convincing that the Atlanta PD tried to link its footage to a string of home invasion robberies from around the time of the film’s release, but the film was ultimately unconnected from the other events. However, Snow was later arrested in May 2016 on charges for aggravated assault.

Cole plays off the film’s realistic filming style, which seemed like documentary footage to many on the surface but ended up being fictional after deeper investigation. He feels that he may be all talk when it comes to the Black Lives Matter movement, as if he has come up short in his support for the movement.

Notably, Cole comes full circle in the last line of the verse. In the first line of the song, he says that he is perceived as “deep” by the public:

Niggas be thinkin' I’m deep, intelligent, fooled by my college degree

While at first he acknowledges that he is deep on the surface, Cole ends the verse by questioning his inner motives, wondering if he really is interpreting the movement to the fullest extent that he can rather than just acting like he is doing so.

J. Cole graduated from St. John’s University in Queens, New York in 2007, earning magna cum laude honors and accruing a 3.82 GPA over his tenure. He detailed his college lifestyle in his May 2007 track, “College Boy,” which was released right as he was graduating from school.

Cole is implying that, although he may have earned a college degree, that doesn’t indicate that he can’t continue to be educated by others who are more aware of things that he is not. This ties into the ensuing lyrics in which he broaches a discussion with Noname. He is also saying that his fans falsely place him on a higher pedestal simply because of his education, but he’s warning them not to.

Interestingly enough, Cole majored in communications with a minor in business, two paths of study that may have helped with both the lyrical side of his career, as he communicates through music, and the managerial side, as he is the owner and co-founder of Dreamville Records.

By invoking the concept of “relatability,” Cole is signaling that despite his “College Boy” intelligence or his aspirations for “grad school,” his core experiences and the hunger in his music are universal to anyone grinding in the “fast life” or the streets. This line functions as a gatekeeper of authenticity, inviting those who understand the pressures of ambition and the hustle to lean in, while simultaneously dismissing anyone who can’t keep up with the grit of his journey. It bridges the gap between Cole’s specific narrative and the broader hip-hop culture of 2007, reinforcing that his lyricism isn’t just an academic exercise but a reflection of a real-world hustle that “real niggas” everywhere can recognize and respect. This sets a tone of mutual understanding, ensuring that when he begins to “split” the competition, his core fan base feels like they are winning right alongside him.

line: (This joint right here is called ”Split You Up”)
meaning: The line (This joint right here is called “Split You Up”) serves as a formal introduction that marks the transition from the narrative-heavy world of College Boy into the pure, unfiltered lyricism of J. Cole’s early career. By explicitly naming the track, Cole adopts a “mixtape host” persona, creating a sense of intimacy and direct communication with his listeners that was a staple of the 2007 era. This announcement signals that the “College Boy” has stepped out of character and back into the booth as a hungry emcee, setting the stage for a display of confidence and competitive fire. It functions as a bold “mission statement,” telling the audience exactly what to expect: a high-energy performance designed to “split” the competition and solidify his reputation as a force to be reckoned with in the rap game. This verbal cue grounds the listener in the moment, making the transition feel like a live performance where Cole is personally guiding you through the journey of The Come Up.

This simple affirmation acts as a transition from the “Gina” storyline into a headspace of pure confidence, where the “College Boy” persona is stripped of its suburban cover to reveal the hungry, competitive spirit of a young J. By leading with this casual yet assertive ad-lib, Cole sets a foundation of “cool” that signals a shift in theme—moving away from domestic deception and toward a more direct, lyrical display of bravado and sexual dominance. Fayettenam is a portmanteau of Fayetteville and Vietnam. meaning:
Cole is literally paid for phrases as a rapper. On the 2019 track “The London,” Cole approximated that he is paid “$2000 every word.” However, Cole’s manager Ibrahim said this number was inaccurate when someone cited it years later.

Cole plays on the human right of freedom of speech/expression while highlighting that speech/expression is becoming increasingly monetized, making it no longer “free” speech. When he states he doesn’t “believe in free speech,” he’s not denying the importance of open expression but pointing out the hypocrisy where speech isn’t always “free” when used as a commodity for profit.

Cole encourages his audience to take him at his word. In 2013, he doubled down on his use of the f-slur on “Villuminati” and apologized for equating “autistic” people to being “retarded” on Drake’s “Jodeci Freestyle”. He asserts that he’s so confident in what he delivers now that he doesn’t need receipts, which are required when customers return purchases they’ve reconsidered.

“Receipts” ties in with his reference to political correctness (PC). During this “Cancel Culture” era, people try to discredit or attack others by exposing new or citing existing information that puts them in an unfavorable light. These pieces of evidence or proof are colloquially known as “receipts”. Expressing his disinterest in political correctness, Cole asks not to bother, as it ultimately won’t phase him.

meaning:
Throughout this verse, Cole narrates his entire life in reverse, beginning with death and rewinding through fame, infidelity, fatherhood, career ambition, childhood, and finally birth. The structure flips the traditional rise narrative on its head, forcing the listener to view success, legacy, and regret backward, where accomplishments dissolve and only the core moments remain.

By telling the story this way, Cole emphasizes how fleeting fame and achievement are. The reverse chronology turns moments that would normally feel triumphant into points of loss and reflection, reinforcing the song’s central question about what truly matters.

Some fans have also noted a possible homage to Nas’ 2001 track “Rewind,” which famously tells a story entirely backward. Given Cole’s long, documented relationship with Nas, including responding to Nas’ criticism of “Work Out” with “Let Nas Down,” this verse may serve as a subtle nod to that influence, and a statement of artistic growth.

In Cole’s life, as his fame increases, his revenue methods and his wealth do too; however, by structuring the verse in reverse, he creates a de-escalation of success. This narrative choice forces the listener to witness the “unmaking” of a superstar. Instead of the traditional “rags to riches” arc, Cole presents “riches to rags,” stripping away the armor of his celebrity, the merchandise, the diverse portfolio, and the guaranteed wins,to reveal the raw struggle underneath. By saying his bank account is “thinnin',” he isn’t describing a failure, but rather a journey back to his hungriest state. Cole leans into the song’s reverse-chronological theme to describe the literal “undoing” of his fatherhood. As time moves backward, his role and memories as a parent are “dispersed”, fading away rather than growing. By “staring at his birth,” Cole is witnessing the moment his son leaves his life to return to the womb, turning what should be a beginning into a tragic, final disappearance.

He could also be referring to his son as is “sun” or the light in his life

line: Now signed to my hero One of the so-called kings of this rap thing that I swear to usurp
vault_lines: now signed to my hero
One of the so-called kings of this rap thing that I swear to usurp
meaning:
Cole reflects on a pivotal moment in his career: signing to JAY-Z’s label Roc Nation in 2009, becoming the first artist ever signed to the imprint. Jay was not only a hero to Cole, but also one of rap’s reigning “kings,” making the deal both symbolic and career-defining.

At the same time, the line captures Cole’s ambition. While he reveres the legends who came before him, he makes it clear he doesn’t intend to stay beneath them. By saying he “swears to usurp,” Cole frames his journey as one of progression, learning from his idols, then striving to surpass them and claim his own place at the top of hip-hop’s hierarchy. Cole even stated this on his Inevitable Podcast in 2024:

“I always was like, ‘This is somebody I idolize and really respect, but I still want to do it on my own.’ I wanted [him to look at me] as a peer [rather than as a little brother].”

line: My life, I see it in reverse I first appeared in a hearse The driver steer to the church My grandkids carry the coffin to the altar as they burst into tears from their shirts
vault_lines: How I see it
, my life, I see it in reverse
I first appeared in a hearse
The driver steer to the church
My grandkids carry the coffin to the altar as they burst into tears from their shirts
meaning:
In this song, Cole literally raps his life story in reverse, “beginning” by imagining his death, basically acknowledging that death is inevitable, just like The Fall-Off…

This concept of telling a story in reverse seems to be inspired by the song ‘Rewind’ by Nas off of his 2001 project ‘Stillmatic’, where he does just that.

A hearse is a vehicle used to carry a coffin at a funeral (no funeral bike, how un-humble). By saying he “first appeared in a hearse,” he frames the song as a reflection on legacy rather than origin. The hearse driving to a church obviously symbolizes a funeral service, but the real weight comes from his grandkids carrying the coffin — saying he lived long enough to build a family and leave something behind.

They burst into tears from their shirt, instead of tears falling to their shirt, because the song is in reverse.

J.Cole’s raps usually involve an element of social commentary, and these few lines paint a harsh but accurate picture of the poverty trap. When living in poverty, there will be a lack of opportunity (luck), high stress (no love) and lack of legitimate employment opportunities (no bucks).

meaning:
Cole illustrates a detailed scene, showing how being aware and knowing when it’s time to go can save your life.

Cole describes a moment in a club where his instincts kick in and he senses danger. “My radar is up” shows he’s alert and aware of his surroundings. The “man with his hat real low” acts as a representation of someone suspicious or potentially violent. Feeling the “negative” energy, he tells the woman he’s with that they need to leave immediately. At the same moment, the lights come on and the DJ grabs the mic, communicating that something has gone wrong (likely a fight, police involvement, or the club shutting down). The scene highlights how quickly a fun night can turn dangerous, tying back into the larger theme of the song, the let out.

meaning:
“The Let Out” refers to the closing time of a nightclub, usually around 2 a.m., where the lights turn on and remaining patrons are kicked out onto the street. The music video for “Two Six” opens with a brief visual of this with this chorus playing over it:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pvf_Qv4rmLM&list=RDpvf_Qv4rmLM&start_radio=1

This transient time period actually marks a handful of Cole’s songs, such as “Deja Vu” from his 2016 album 4 Your Eyez Only where the chorus repeats:

Club jumping, don’t stop, off top
But you know we only go ‘til 2 o'clock
[…]
Last call at the bar, ladies get a drink, nigga get some balls
Ain’t no telling you gon’ see that bitch tomorrow
Stop holding up the wall waiting for the right song
Better holla ‘cause you know they 'bout to cut the lights on

To that, “Last Call,” the final track on Cole’s 2009 mixtape The Warm Up, is named after the time that clubs stop serving alcohol, which is usually a few hours before or the same as “The Let Out.” As Cole alludes to, this is a dangerous time for him to be seen, as he’s more vulnerable to being robbed or killed in the exhaustion and confusion of the crowded late night.

By the time of The Fall-Off (2026)’s release, The Sims series was an already established and well-known brand whose gaming concept of life simulation had been shaping popular culture for over two decades. Finally, considering the game’s concept, Cole is saying real world would be just God’s game and we are all insignificant characters of it. This also connects to an actual existencial hypothesis called the Simulation Argument, by philosopher Nick Bostrom.

line: What would I do with no team? I wouldn’t do anything I would just sit on this music and hold it Waiting for some perfect moment Wondering why it ain’t came Meanwhile the world done changed Suddenly songs I was loving last year don’t feel the same Somebody feel my pain

Suddenly songs I was loving last year don't feel the same

Please, somebody say I changed
meaning:
Without the support around him, Cole would likely succumb to his inner critic and remain petrified by perfectionism. This means repeatedly missing his moment—losing enthusiasm for songs of his own that he once loved, but now views as subpar and perhaps sounding outdated. Without his team pushing him to release these, they may all have remained stuck in an endless loop of eventual displeasure and obsessive refinement to a fleeting standard of perfection.

In his “Applying Pressure: The Off-Season Documentary”, this is precisely the backstory Cole gives us for “MIDDLE CHILD”:

There are songs on here in this whole Fall-Off era that I’ve been sitting on for years, just tweaking, making better, even like a “Middle Child”, that was for The Fall-Off… So we put out “Middle Child” as a single, now normally I would just hoard that song, and similarly yes I’ve been hoarding songs because I’m like, I made this for The Fall-Off, this is too special, now over the years, they have gotten better, I still got more work to do, especially on The Fall Off specifically, got a few more songs to write, I got more tinkering I need to do.

It’s possible that “Everybody Dies” and “False Prophets” were ultimately culled from The Fall-Off’s eventual track list under similar pressure from his team to simply release the tracks rather than endlessly hoard and refine them.

line: [Verse 2: J. Cole]

meaning:
Cole is known for being outwardly humble–he doesn’t make ostentatious displays of wealth–but here mentions a 5 star hotel “The Mandarin Oriental” located in New York City’s Columbus Circle that still fails to meet his elevated, selective lifestyle standards. He’s so bougie and has stayed there so often that this expensive hotel isn’t even nice enough–it’s old and no longer interesting to him.





So instead, for his houses Cole doesn’t even purchase pre-built “cribs,” he is wealthy enough that he has them built to his exact specifications.

However, one instance of J Cole building rather than merely buying cribs would be his own childhood home, which reflects a less superficial and more self-defined conception of luxury. This would be Fayetteville, the “2-6,” the city where J Cole grew up with his single mother on 2014 Forest Hills Drive (the namesake of his 2014 album). When repurchasing the house in 2014, he specially repurposed it to accommodate rent-free housing for single mothers.



Cole maintains a common thread throughout Verse 2 in Two Six, which is his subversion of purely superficial pursuits like chasing the bag, flaunting wealth to appear bougie, and going viral off clout and fame. Instead, his level of luxury takes on a more refined style. He is both literally “bougie” and “bougie” internally, valuing self-defined luxury, freedom to live at one’s own standards, and an authentic life.

By saying someone got a speech impediment from “cuddling choppers,” Cole suggests that constant exposure to gun violence has left him permanently marked. meaning:
Cole draws a parallel between generations by reframing addiction. In the 1990s, crack cocaine was the destructive force tearing through communities; today, he argues that clout and fame play a similar role. Attention has become the new drug, something people chase compulsively.

He criticizes how social media incentivizes negativity, with people getting “gassed” off going viral through hate, outrage, or controversy. To Cole, this shift is a disgrace, fame is no longer earned through skill or substance, but through whatever behavior generates the most attention, even if it’s corrosive.

This newly evolved cultural poison was also addressed by Cole on “Bronx Zoo Freestyle” off Birthday Blizzard ‘26, an EP of freestyles released 11 days before The Fall-Off:

meaning:
2-6 is one of the nicknames locals have given to a military base located in Fayetteville, NC. The number “26” has been and still is being used as the jail code or area identifier for Cumberland County, Fayetteville, NC.

Locals coined the nickname “Fayettenam” because they didn’t want the military base to be shipped out to Vietnam during the war, and because of the high crime rate during the war era. The name is still used today, with one of its other nicknames being “2-6.” Cole himself is also from Fayetteville.

The chorus of “Two Six” also samples The Last Mr. Bigg’s 1999 song, “Trial Time,” in which Bigg sings:

Take that shit to trial, bitch
Take that shit to trial

In addition, Cole released The Fall-Off on February 6th, 2026, which includes both the numbers 2 and 6. He also pays homage to Dreamville artist JID by referencing “Bruddannem,” one of JID’s songs.

meaning:
Cole first coined the phrase “Ville mentality” back in 2013 on the track “Can I Holla At Ya?” from his Truly Yours EP. The term represents a self-defeating outlook in the face of limited opportunity. Instead of ever chasing their dreams, the victims of said mentality instead prescribe to the same cycle of violence or self destruction as the previous generation. He examined a similar idea on “Foldin' Clothes,” where he compared people who succumb, to actors—they never reveal their true feelings.

He further expanded on this idea in his Forest Hills Drive: Homecoming documentary:

I realized the opportunity is in your mentality … I didn’t necessarily have to leave Fayetteville to do what I did. You can be great in this place and make this place great.

line: Like once they get a hit of this, they hooked like that Twitter shit
vault_lines: Like once they get a hit of this, they hooked like that Twitter shit
meaning:
Cole likens the impact of his music to a drug: once listeners get a “hit,” they’re hooked. He extends the metaphor to Twitter, comparing the addictive pull of his songs to the way people get “hooked” on social media.

When this line dropped in 2009, conversations around social media addiction weren’t nearly as mainstream as they are today. Looking back, it feels prophetic. Platforms like Twitter are designed to keep users engaged through dopamine-triggering rewards like likes, retweets, and notifications, and endless scrolling that makes it hard to stop. Just as drugs manipulate brain chemistry to keep people coming back, social media thrives on the same cycle of highs and withdrawals.

Cole would revisit this theme almost a decade later on his 2018 track “Photograph,” which wrestles with the shallow connections and compulsions created by apps like Instagram. In the same year, he admitted in an interview with Angie Martinez that he had his own struggles with social media addiction, reinforcing how prescient this early bar really was:

meaning:
The opening lines (“Who’s on my side and who’s obliged for closin’ my curtains…”)
evoke Pac’s growing distrust after the 1994 Quad Studios shooting. The imagery of “closin’ my curtains” suggests betrayal from within people close enough to protect him potentially setting him up instead. The “mist with clinched fists” captures Pac’s mental fog: anger and confusion hardening into militancy. When he says he “picked up this sword” it’s metaphorical, choosing lyrical (and possibly real) warfare over reconciliation.

“I know there’s money in violence… profit in war” is Cole’s meta-commentary on how the East Coast–West Coast feud became commodified. Diss tracks, magazine covers, and label politics turned personal pain into marketable drama. Pac recognizes that conflict sells but still feels personally abandoned.

“But, shit, I felt that you left me to hang, I gave you game” references Pac’s belief that he mentored Biggie early on, sharing industry advice before Biggie’s rise. “Rap for the bitches” points to Pac’s criticism that Biggie pivoted toward more radio-friendly, commercially viable content.

When Pac says Biggie’s “content resemblin’ mine, it brought you fame,” it reflects the accusation that Biggie borrowed stylistic or thematic elements from him. Yet Cole complicates the bitterness: “I didn’t complain, I cheered you on.” This suggests admiration and pride that later curdled into resentment.

“At the same time, my destiny brought me pain / From kickin’ it with some venomous niggas…” acknowledges Pac’s own flawed choices, aligning with dangerous figures (implicitly Suge Knight and Death Row affiliates). “The same ones that you warned me ’bout” reframes Biggie not as a villain, but as someone who may have genuinely cautioned him. This deepens the tragedy: Pac ignored advice due to pride and paranoia.

“The trigger squeezed, my paranoia noticed you in the vicinity” captures the heart of the feud. Whether literal (Quad Studios) or metaphorical, Pac’s trauma makes him see Biggie everywhere, even without proof. Cole highlights how trauma distorts perception; suspicion fills informational gaps.

“When they sentenced me / Lawyers milked me for every penny…” references Pac’s prison sentence and financial exploitation. Stripped of power and freedom, all he has is memory, and fear. “…all I had inside that cell was my memory is said in a way that references the Pac line, "All I got left is stinkin' memories” from Life Goes On. “The fear that while I’m gone, they forgettin’ me”** exposes a core insecurity beneath the bravado, irrelevance. In a fast-moving industry, prison meant silence, and silence meant possibly being replaced, perhaps by Biggie himself.

By writing from Pac’s perspective, he humanizes both men and reframes their conflict not as pure hatred, but as wounded pride, industry manipulation, survivor’s guilt, and the corrosive effects of fame. The verse becomes less about who was right and more about how two generational talents were pushed into a narrative that profited everyone except them.

line: Instead of escalatin’
meaning:
“What’s up, Pac? / I heard that record that you did that just dropped / It’s bubblin’, got me wonderin’ when the love stopped”
Biggie opens casually and calmly, signaling maturity rather than hostility.
“That record” refers to Hit ’Em Up, Tupac’s explosive diss track aimed at Biggie and Bad Boy Records.
“It’s bubblin’” acknowledges the song’s growing buzz and impact in the streets.
“Wonderin’ when the love stopped” reflects on their once friendly relationship. Before the East Coast–West Coast rivalry peaked, Biggie and Pac were collaborators and friends. This line emphasizes confusion and hurt rather than anger.
Cole reframes the feud as a tragic misunderstanding rather than inevitable warfare.

“‘Hit ’Em Up,’ I’m like, maybe I should / Write you before shit go left, the streets is a bit upset”
Biggie considers de-escalation instead of retaliation. “Hit ‘Em Up” in this context is a triple entendre
1. It means Big heard the Tupac diss
2. He’s questioning whether he should respond back and fuel the beef
3. He’s saying Let me call Tupac and solve this peacefully.
Rather than responding with another diss, he thinks about writing Pac privately.
“Before shit go left” suggests stopping things before they spiral into violence.
“The streets is a bit upset” references how fans, media, and entourages amplified the tension. In the 90s, hip-hop beef wasn’t just lyrical, it had real-world consequences.
Cole implies that ego and outside pressure fueled the conflict more than the artists themselves.

“You claimin’ that you fucked my bitch, but, check / Instead of escalatin’”
This references one of the most infamous lines in Hit ’Em Up: “That’s why I fucked your bitch, you fat motherfucker.”
Biggie acknowledges the disrespect but pauses to think rationally.
“But, check” signals he’s about to respond thoughtfully instead of emotionally.
Cole humanizes Biggie here, he portrays him as someone capable of restraint, not just pride.

“At a time when niggas say, ‘Big, let’s decimate ’em’ / I’m tellin’ ’em ‘Chill’”
This highlights peer pressure from Biggie’s circle and the broader East Coast camp.
“Decimate ’em” captures the competitive, warlike energy surrounding the feud.
Biggie choosing to say “Chill” suggests leadership and foresight.

Cole’s larger theme, one moment of maturity could have altered hip-hop history. Cole is likely using this story to explain his own recent actions, specifically stepping away from the Kendrick Lamar and Drake feud. He’s saying that just because everyone wants to see a fight doesn’t mean you have to give them one. He’d rather be the guy who says “chill” than the guy who ends up as a tragic headline.

meaning:
In this outro the girl interviewed in the song’s intro continues to speak about her cousin’s near-death in a gun crime incident, explaining that she believes God himself spared her cousin’s life and the proof for that is that he’s still alive.

The interviewer replies to the girl by posing a question that echoes the famous philosophical dilemma of The Problem Of Evil, which can be summed up by the question “How can we reconcile the existence of an All-Loving, omniscient and omnipotent God with the existence of evil in the world?”

The Problem of Evil is one of the most famous objections to the existence of God and to the monotheistic religions, which are founded upon the notion of a single creator and almighty God.

On popular culture, it has been explored by the late David Foster Wallace in part of his famous 2005 Kenyon College Commencement Address, informally named This Is Water.

line: Down and confused, I know What I reap is what I will sow

meaning:
“You reap what you sow” comes from the principle of sowing and reaping, a practice of working the ground to gain a harvest, which is nearly old as humanity itself was. Adam in the Bible himself, learned that it was a part of his curse, so he was familiar with it as well.

It means that all of your actions will have to face consequences within themselves. It is also an idiom that references two Bible verses in the New Testament.

2 Corinthians 9:6 describes it steps of sowing sparingly and bountifully.

But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.

meaning:
The narrator finally questions his own sanity, realizing his addictive tendencies of always wanting more materialistic pleasures. This shows a growth of his mentality from the title track of the album:

Don’t give a fuck and I’m somewhat insane

He thought his problems would be fixed once he obtained these things, as shown in “ATM” where he vents his monetary urges:

Don’t wanna fall off so I’m all in my bag
Thankin' God like it’s biblical
I know it’s gon' solve every problem I have

The narrator now—while sitting in his Range Rover, a very expensive luxury vehicle—realizes that no amount of money, drugs, or possessions can mitigate his inner troubles. This reinforces the messages of valuing self-appreciation and love taught in Cole’s music.

This isn’t the first time Cole has stressed the fact that money can’t buy happiness. One of his many hit songs, “Love Yourz”, off of the certified-platinum album 2014 Forest Hills Drive, speaks on this belief of his, with the often quoted line “Think bein broke was better.”

line: All I ever wanted was to hear them bitches holler back Get some money plus respect and now look, I got all of that

Get some money plus respect and now look, I got all of that
meaning:
A product of the horrendous environment he grew up in, the narrator ultimately reflects on why he is the way he is.

He only craved to experience the things he was insecure about being denied. Those insecurities barred him from settling for the love of a spouse, so he tried finding solace in a life of luxary that only exacerbated his feelings of emptiness. That emptiness ultimately fueled his drug addiction.

In retrospect, all the narrator really wanted was to fulfill his self-esteem, he just chased that fulfillment in the wrong things. This strongly echoes the sentiment of the lines in 2014’s “Love Yourz”:

The good news is, nigga, you came a long way
The bad news is, nigga, you went the wrong way

These lines also draw parallels to that of Cozz’s 2017 song, “Zendaya” where Cole rapped about music serving as a major inspiration for the majority of his life:

Cole would later fulfill his dream when his sophomore album, Born Sinner was certified platinum on February 9, 2016 by the RIAA. This would be followed by a much larger award when his third and most successful album, 2014 Forest Hillz Drive, which notably contained zero features, would be certified double platinum on October 22nd of the same year.

meaning:
Cole reflects on growing up in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where intense Southern heat is a daily reality. Saying “you could melt” emphasizes how extreme the environment is, to the point where it feels life-threatening.

The line also carries street-level wordplay. “Heat” is common slang for a gun, and “melt” can mean being killed. Read this way, Cole is subtly suggesting that in his environment, the heat isn’t just the weather, it’s the violence that surrounds it. The idea that “summer humidity enhances stupidity” reinforces how harsh conditions can fuel reckless decisions with deadly consequences.

meaning:
Cole contrasts two paths he faced early on. “Class-8 tempos” refers to driving heavy-duty trucks (Class 8 commercial vehicles), a stable but demanding blue-collar route. By saying he chose rapping over that, Cole highlights the risk he took in pursuing music instead of a more conventional, reliable career.

The second line places this decision in a specific era of hip-hop, before social media made breaking out easier. At the time, aspiring rappers had to physically pass demos to A&R reps in hopes of being signed. Cole is emphasizing how early he committed to rap, choosing the grind of chasing industry gatekeepers over a safer, traditional job.

JAY-Z and Kanye West are two of J. Cole’s major musical influences. In a 2011 interview with Nessa, he cited Jay as one of his favorite rappers growing up, and as of this song’s release he’s signed to Jay’s Roc Nation record label.

Despite Cole’s later disillusionment with Kanye on 2016’s “False Prophets,” Cole drew inspiration from Ye’s music while he was on the come-up, as he expressed in a 2010 interview with Vulture:

I’m such a Kanye West fan. I would love to work with him on a major scale. Not just a song here or a song there I would love to do something extraordinary with him, but I feel like I gotta step my game up and kind of earn my spot before I can worry about that.

In the phrase “yea high,” the word “yea” essentially means “this”—it’s used to estimate the unknown height of an object, or in this case a person. Cole’s using the term to note that his love for rap music began early in his childhood. In a 2010 discussion with DJ Whoo Kid, he revealed he was inspired to start rapping by listening to Eminem and Cannibus in the late 1990s and early 2000s:

I don’t know if I’m on his radar yet, but I used to hang Eminem raps on my wall. I have people’s raps on my wall, but his raps and then Canibus' raps were the only ones that could get close to the bedspread and when I’d first wake up and want to read some raps, they were always there.

line: Penitentiary chances just to make a couple bucks
vault_lines: Penitentiary chances just to make a couple bucks
meaning:
“Penitentiary chances” are high-risk, illegal acts that could lead to jail time or imprisonment. 21 Savage says he is willing to take these risks for any dollar amount.

Taking “penitentiary chances” is a common trope in hip-hop, but the phrase finds one of its earliest uses on a medium in a 1907 issue of McClure’s Magazine, where it discusses professional criminals in Chicago who were willing to risk going to jail in order to help politicians get votes in certain wards.

After 1907, the phrase is seen again in Sterling B. Scott’s 1994 novel The Weeds of Society. The narrator at one point says:

No longer would I be a small-time street hustler taking penitentiary chances for nickels and dimes.

The last piece of media that seems to use this outside of rap is a 1998 low-budget indie film directed by Quiroz brothers, Jose and Eduardo, called Penitentiary Chances. The film is a prequel to Veteranos and is credited with being the beginning of the urban movie genre. It can be viewed in its entirety on YouTube.

line: Question How many faking they streams? (A lot) Getting they plays from machines? (A lot)
vault_lines: How many faking they streams? (A lot)
Getting they plays from machines? (A lot)
meaning:
In mid-2010, the “album equivalent unit” was introduced to count streams and downloads as album sales. Subsequently, streaming scandals grew exceptionally over the years. A number of trends such as extremely long albums, streaming playlist, and song loops all focus on the album-equivalent unit—1 album sale = 10 song downloads = 1250 song streams on a paid platform.

The use of excessive tracklists can be seen on Chris Brown’s 45-track project Heartbreak on a Full Moon and Migos' Culture II. The more streams per song means more revenue for the artist, leading to massive tracklists.

Another scandal, song loops, can be seen with Post Malone’s “rockstar” and Migos' “MotorSport.” In October 2017, The FADER reported that Republic Records uploaded a chorus loop to Post’s “rockstar” to YouTube, helping gain over 65 million additional streams.

In addition, record labels also manipulate streams by using “machines” or bots—artificial intelligence that repeatedly plays songs for no audience. For example, multiple streams at the same time and albums being played all day to create artificial streams. In mid-2018, Tidal was also accused of falsifying and manipulating its streams.

Artist James Montgomery Flagg’s 1917 poster used to recruit soldiers in America for both World War I and World War II.

Aesthetically, the flamboyant, striking graphic design of the poster elicited strong emotions within the people at the time; it played upon their fears, vexation, and possible faith in freedoms that lingered in their minds during the war. However, what lurks beneath the radiant poster is a message that seemingly calls for the population to endure personal sacrifices and domestic adjustments to further national agenda.

When it’s time for ex-servicemen to get out, they are often afraid of going back to their roots as this means they must face reality once again – that they must do better. Unfortunately, they would often rather make the easy choice of comfortability and return to what they know, instead of taking the heard route which would reap them more rewards in the future.

meaning:
Cole candidly admits to having envied wealthy people in the past. Rather than pretending he was always above that mindset, he acknowledges that jealousy once tempted him, but overcoming it was necessary for his own growth and prosperity.

He explored similar feelings on 2013 track “Rich Niggaz”, where he reflected on resenting wealthy people while growing up. In a 2013 interview discussing the song, Cole explained:

I used to have such a problem, with like, with people with money. It was almost a bitterness and a jealousy because my mom got to work so hard.

Cole additionally argues that envy is ultimately self-defeating. The line “Envy keep your pockets empty” suggests that obsessing over other people’s success distracts from building your own, while the image of broke people mocking millionaires highlights the irony of criticizing the very success they secretly desire.

At the same time, Cole pushes back against the cliché that “money isn’t everything.” While a central message of his magnum opus 2014 Forest Hills Drive is that money and fame don’t necessarily solve every problem or bring happiness, he points out that many critics of wealthy people would pursue money just as aggressively, perhaps even more immorally than he did, if given the opportunity.

The chorus is another nod to Fayetteville. It features the chant from the song “Fayetteville (F-A-Y-E-T-T-E-V-I-DOUBLE-L-E)” by the group Ground Zero. https://www.soundclick.com/music/songinfo_standalone/?songID=2831114

The chorus also serves as a rhythmic chant of reclamation. By repeating “The motherfuckin' Ville” with increasing intensity, Cole is essentially drilling his origin into the listener’s head, turning a local nickname into a global anthem. It functions as a “sonic flag,” planting his feet firmly in Fayetteville regardless of where the music is being played.

The spelling out of “F-A-Y-E-T-T-E-V-I double L-E” is a callback to classic hip-hop tropes where rappers spell out their names or cities to show pride (similar to how “N-E-W-Y-O-R-K” is often chanted). By doing this three times, Cole isn’t just naming a place; he’s performing a ritual of unapologetic loyalty.

vault_lines: The Son of Man extendin' his hand to Son of Sam
In forgiveness for all of the homicides we witnessed
meaning:
In comparing himself to the bullet directed at President Donald Trump during a failed July 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, Cole makes another allusion to the act of murder and the concept of salvation.

David Berkowitz, widely known by the alias “Son of Sam”, committed a string of homicides in New York City from 1976-1977 and caused a wave of terror and paranoia among the populace before he was eventually arrested. Berkowitz, notably, became a born-again Christian after being sentenced to life imprisonment.

In extending one’s hand to someone, it is perceived as an act of assistance or goodwill. Cole, in this case, likens himself to Jesus Christ, or the “Son of Man”, because he is seen as one of the tenets of the Holy Spirit in Christianity, with Jesus acting as an extension of God. God, furthermore, is seen in Christianity as the only entity who can offer forgiveness, grant eternal salvation and ultimately absolve a person of their sins, provided that the person confesses and expresses repentance.

On the surface, one may wonder why a person such as “Son of Sam” should deserve forgiveness for multiple instances of murder, given that he took the lives of multiple people and left thousands of people in a state of paranoia during his spree. Cole, however, uses Berkowitz as an example to convey the message that human beings are not inherently wicked and that instead of demonizing people on the basis of their misdeeds for their rest of their lives, as well as in perpetuity after their deaths, society should instead strive towards granting people forgiveness while understanding the factors that led them towards committing undesirable acts so that they can be remedied for future generations.

He dubbed the spot “Mohammed crib” because his landlord, who kept him off the streets by allowing him to continually miss his rent, was named Muhammad:

meaning:
J. Cole came from modest beginnings. His father left him at a young age, and his mother delved into drug abuse to cope with depression. On 2018’s “Once an Addict (Interlude),” Cole recalls his mother’s struggle:

Callin' me at 12 at night
She drunk as fuck and I’m upset
‘Cause why she always using me for crutch?
Growin’ up I used to always see her up
Late as shit, cigarette smoke and greatest hits from Marvin Gaye

Cole worked part-time jobs before pursuing rap. His hopes of becoming a rapper led to him waiting three hours outside of JAY-Z’s studio to hand him a CD. He signed with Roc Nation in 2009. In an interview with The Morning After, Cole told the story:

I was telemarketing for a really small newspaper in Queens. […] So I saw the press release that he was coming out with American Gangsta and everything was going so fast. And I’m like ‘Yo, you know what? I bet he’s still kinda making a few joints, like a few more joints.’ I had an idea for a song. I went home that day made a beat which I think is incredible, it’s called ‘Top of the World’ […] we made a beat CD, I got a hook on it and everything. […] I told E matter of fact, I’m like ‘Yo, I bet he’s gon’ probably be at the studio tonight.‘ […] At that time he was at Rock the mic. […] We were just sitting outside for like two hours drinking, it started raining. I’m sitting there with a beat CD, t-shirt on and a bottle, just waiting, just praying that JAY’s going to show up. So about two hours later, we see this black Phantom come over. […] JAY gets out of the car, walks up to the building and I’m like trying to build up the nerve to go up to him with the CD. […] So I’m just like, I’m like 'Yo JAY, yo huh, yo huh I got this.’ He was like ‘What is this? Like what is this?’ He was like ‘Give it to one of those guys.’

Since then, Cole has become one of the best-known rappers in hip-hop. His April 2018 album KOD racked up 397.000 copies sold in the first week, proving his spot at the top of the game.

meaning:
Cole reflects on his family’s history of substance abuse, noting how addiction was often used as a coping mechanism for depression and hardship. He’s been candid about his mother’s struggles with alcoholism throughout his career, perhaps most poignantly on 2018’s “Once An Addict (Interlude).”

Here, he admits that because he came from a family of users rather than hustlers, the instincts to make money in the streets weren’t naturally there. Surrounded by examples of people self-medicating rather than grinding, he often found himself broke and envying the kids who were hustling and rocking the freshest gear. This directly recalls 2014’s “03’ Adolescence”, where Cole told the story of asking a friend to put him on out of jealousy.

Ironically, it may have been that very envy that fueled his eventual rise to the top. Today, Cole has amassed an estimated $60 million net worth and is regarded as a top three rapper of his generation. But his journey highlights a paradox: the people we envy for their material wealth or external success are often driven by deep insecurities, feeling their lives don’t have value unless validated by extreme achievement. Leading up to his magnum opus 2014 Forest Hills Drive, Cole often admitted in interviews that he believed fame, accolades, and money would bring happiness, but eventually realized that mindset was empty. That lesson culminated in the album’s closer “Love Yourz”, where Cole realizes true fulfillment comes not from material success, but from appreciating the blessings already in your life. As he explained in a 2015 interview with Tavis Smiley:

When I was young, I thought success was all I needed… buying my mom a house, the fame, the accolades. I thought those would be the things that bring happiness. And when those things came, the happiness wasn’t there.
[…]
You’re so focused on the next step, the next success… that you forget the only things that matter – that’s your mother, that’s family, that’s love.

meaning:
J. Cole details the harsh realities of hood life, describing how frequently death and tragedy take place. According to Police Procedure, the fact that these bodies are placed in morgues suggests that they did not die of natural causes and are being held by a medical examiner for autopsy.

In order to emphasize the horrors of gun violence in America, Cole compares the number of gun-related deaths to total US deaths in WWII. In 2017, 39,773 people died due to gun-related injuries, while there was a total number of 418,500 US deaths during WWII. Although WWII was the deadliest military conflict in history, resulting in the estimated deaths of over 70 million—3% of the world’s population in 1940—the US suffered fewer casualties compared to other nations because of the location of the war and its late entry.



Additionally, there is research which supports Cole’s claim about the scope of gun violence in America. An August 2015 Politifact article found that there have been 1.5 million gun-related deaths since 1968, compared to 1.3 million war deaths since the American Revolution—corroborating a December 2012 statement made by PBS commentator Mark Shields:

[Since 1968], more Americans have died from gunfire than died in all the wars of this country’s history…

line: One phone call get you canceled like a homophobe in this PC culture
vault_lines: One phone call get you canceled like a homophobe in this PC culture
meaning:
J. Cole mentions his disdain for cancel culture, which he is no stranger to despite his humble persona. He seems to insinuate that cancellation due to political correctness (PC) culture does more harm than good. However, he is also saying that he has the power to cancel someone with a single phone call.

Cole was impacted by cancel culture about a month before dropping this song. It came from the surprise release of his June 2020 single, “Snow on tha Bluff,” which was a response to public criticism that he was receiving from Chicago rapper Noname. Cole was accused of misogyny for the track’s timing and lyrics.

Although this was a recent situation, Cole had been impacted by cancel culture several times between 2013 and 2014. He was previously accused of being homophobic after playfully using a slur on his June 2013 track, “Villuminati,” but he doubled down on his intentional use of the word when questioned.

Only four days after that song’s release, he faced additional backlash for his insensitive lyrics about autism on Drake’s “Jodeci Freestyle.” Cole quickly apologized for his bars at the time, and they were edited out when Drake re-released the song on streaming services in 2019.

Lastly, Cole was also accused of misogyny for his December 2014 track, “No Role Modelz,” but this never became a major controversy.

meaning:
Cole plays on his last name being homophonic with coal; this rock turns into a diamond when put under pressure, which Cole mentions in the previous line. He has used the same analogy on several previous songs, like his May 2011 track, “Return of Simba”:

Cole under pressure, what that make? Diamonds

He rapped a similar line on Dreamville’s June 2019 single, “Down Bad”:

Ville nigga, I was born in the same
Pressure cooker that’s been known to bust a lump of coal and make a diamond

Cole seems to be saying that, when under pressure, he makes valuable music, some that could even be certified diamond. A record receives this certification when it sells ten million copies, and while Cole has yet to achieve this as of this song’s release, he is a multi-platinum selling artist and is well on his way to eventually accomplishing the feat.

“I’m quotin' gold” does recognize the many gold and platinum certifications that Cole has attained at this point in his career. It also alludes to how profitable his lyrics are, something that Cole expressed on Young Thug’s May 2019 single, “The London”:

line: Made a lil’ tune called “Foldin Clothes,” and a nigga still ain’t known to fold under pressure
vault_lines: Made a lil' tune called "Foldin Clothes," and a nigga still ain't known to fold under pressure
meaning:
J. Cole calls back to his December 2016 track, “Foldin Clothes,” which is about the things that he does out of love for his wife, such as folding their clothes after they’re washed.

Cole highlights the irony of having an entire song written about “folding” while still not being known to fold under pressure as “to fold” means to switch up in or back out of a difficult situation.

Cole could be alluding to his abrupt dispute with Chicago rapper Noname, which transpired about a month before this song’s release. In a contentious tweet, she seemingly criticized Cole and Kendrick Lamar for their social media silence amidst protests of police brutality, and Cole decided to respond in song with “Snow on tha Bluff.” Even after receiving immense criticism for the single’s lyrics and timing, Cole was firm in his stance and said that he stood “behind every word.”

line: Turn up your decibels, peep how I decimate a joint Check out my projects like them workers that Section 8 appoints And you’ll see how I flipped like exclamation points
vault_lines: Turn up your decibels, peep how I decimate a joint
Check out my projects like them workers that Section 8 appoints
And you'll see how I flipped like exclamation points
meaning:
Following the preceding line, J. Cole uses wordplay with punctuation. While ‘decimate’ literally means to destroy something, it ties back into the decimal that was mentioned above. He proceeds with “appoint,” so both “decimal” and “point” are about the period punctuation mark.

Section 8 housing is a federally subsidized program for poor or low-income families. Such buildings are commonly known as “the projects,” but that word secondarily represents Cole’s full-length releases.

Furthering the punctuation scheme, Cole mentions the exclamation mark, which, when horizontally flipped, resembles the letter “i.” However, inverted exclamation marks are also used in written Spanish. “Flipped” could additionally allude to Cole sampling another artist’s music in his instrumentals, otherwise known as “flipping” a sample.
